title: Carré d'Agneau Persillé with Pommes Anna
summary: A French-trimmed rack of lamb, seared, brushed with Dijon and coated in a green crust of breadcrumbs, parsley and garlic, roasted pink and carved into cutlets, with pommes Anna, a cake of thinly sliced potatoes cooked in clarified butter until golden. It is in the Chef course because frenching a rack, roasting to the degree and turning out a perfect potato cake are three classic skills on one plate.
skills: pommes Anna sliced thin and layered
equipment: 10 inch (25 cm) heavy ovenproof frying pan, ideally cast iron, for the pommes Anna
Second heavy frying pan for searing
Small saucepan and fine sieve for clarifying butter
Food processor or a sharp knife for the crumb
A heavy saucepan lid or a second pan to press the potatoes

ingredients.note: ask for the chine bone removed
1 tbsp (15 ml) for the jus, 2 tbsp (30 ml) for searing

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, melted, for the crumb

ingredients.note: makes about 1/2 cup (100 g) clarified butter

ingredients.item: Starchy-waxy potatoes such as Yukon Gold or Maris Piper

mise: Clarify the butter: melt it slowly, skim the foam, and pour the clear yellow fat away from the milky solids at the bottom.
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
Blitz the breadcrumbs, parsley, garlic and thyme until fine and bright green, then stir in the melted butter and a pinch of salt.
Take the lamb out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking.

timeline.do: Clarify the butter; french the racks; start the jus.
Slice potatoes; build and start the pommes Anna (45 to 55 minutes).
Make the green crumb.
Sear the lamb, mustard and crumb it.
Roast the lamb 15 to 20 minutes; turn out the potatoes.
Rest the lamb; cut the pommes Anna.
Carve and plate.

steps.do: French the racks: stand each rack with the bones pointing up and score a line across the fat 2 inches (5 cm) from the bone tips. Cut down to the bone along that line, then cut away all the fat and meat from the top of the bones. Scrape each bone clean with the back of the knife and rub with kitchen paper to remove the membrane.
steps.look: Clean, white bone tips and a neat eye of meat with a thin layer of fat.
steps.mistake: Leaving bits of meat and membrane on the bones, which burn black in the oven.
steps.fix: Scrape again with the knife held at a right angle to the bone; a rough cloth helps rub off the last of the membrane.

steps.do: Trim the fat cap on top of the eye to about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick and score it lightly in a crisscross. Season the racks all over with salt and pepper.
steps.look: A thin, even fat cap and a well-seasoned rack.
steps.mistake: Leaving thick fat, which will not render under the crust.
steps.fix: Trim more; you want just enough to baste the meat.

steps.do: Make a quick jus: brown the trimmings from frenching in 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the oil in a small saucepan over medium-high heat for 6 to 8 minutes, add the shallot for 2 minutes, pour in the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) stock and simmer for 20 to 25 minutes until reduced to about 1/2 cup (120 ml). Strain, skim off the fat and season.
steps.look: Deep brown trimmings, then a stock that reduces to a glossy, savoury jus that coats a spoon thinly.
steps.mistake: Boiling the stock hard with the fat still on it, which clouds and greases the jus.
steps.fix: Keep it at a steady simmer, let it stand 1 minute off the heat and spoon the fat off before straining.

steps.do: Slice the potatoes 1/16 inch (2 mm) thick on the mandoline. Do not rinse them: the starch glues the cake. Toss in a bowl with 1/3 cup (75 g) clarified butter, 1 tsp (5 g) salt and pepper.
steps.look: Thin, translucent rounds, coated and glistening.
steps.mistake: Rinsing the slices, which washes away the starch so the cake falls apart.
steps.fix: Use the slices straight from the mandoline.

steps.do: Pour 2 tbsp (25 g) clarified butter into the cold ovenproof pan. Arrange the slices in overlapping concentric circles, starting from the centre, each layer turning the opposite direction, until all are used. Press firmly with a heavy lid.
steps.look: A neat spiral of potatoes, tightly layered, about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) thick.
steps.mistake: Laying the slices loosely, so the cake will not hold together.
steps.fix: Press each layer down hard as you go.

steps.do: Cook on the stove over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes until you hear a steady sizzle and see the edges turn golden. Cover with buttered foil, press down, and bake at 425°F (220°C) for 30 minutes, then uncover and bake 15 to 20 minutes more until a knife slides through with no resistance.
steps.look: Golden, crisp edges, the cake slightly shrunk from the pan side.
steps.mistake: Skipping the stove-top start, so the base is pale.
steps.fix: Return the pan to the stove for 3 to 5 minutes to brown the base before turning out.

steps.do: Heat the remaining 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the second pan over medium-high heat and sear the racks fat side down for 3 to 4 minutes until golden, then sear the meat side for 1 minute. Hold the bones out of the pan.
steps.look: Golden, rendered fat and a crust on the eye.
steps.mistake: Searing the bones, which blackens them.
steps.fix: Lean the racks against the side of the pan to keep the bones clear.

steps.do: Let the racks cool for 5 minutes, then brush the fat side and the eye with Dijon mustard and press on the green crumb in an even layer, about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.look: A bright green, compact crust.
steps.mistake: Pressing the crumb onto a hot, greasy rack, so it slides off.
steps.fix: Cool the racks a little and blot excess fat before the mustard.

steps.do: Stand the racks on the rack in the roasting tray, bones interlocked like crossed swords, and roast at 425°F (220°C) for 15 to 20 minutes until the centre reads 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C) for medium-rare.
steps.look: A crisp, golden-green crust; the meat yielding when pressed.
steps.mistake: Overcooking it to grey; lamb is best pink.
steps.fix: Check from 12 minutes; pull when the thermometer reaches 125°F (52°C).

steps.do: Rest the racks for 8 minutes. Meanwhile, slide a palette knife round the pommes Anna, put a board over the pan and turn it out in one confident movement.
steps.look: A golden-brown cake with a neat spiral on top.
steps.mistake: Turning out a cake that is stuck, so it tears.
steps.fix: Loosen all round with the palette knife and let it stand 2 minutes first; any stuck slices can be patched back on.

steps.do: Carve the racks between the bones into single or double cutlets with a sharp knife, holding the crust with your fingers so it does not break. Cut the potato cake into wedges with a serrated knife, and finish everything with flaky salt.
steps.look: Rosy pink meat edge to edge, a crisp green crust, and clean cuts.
steps.mistake: Sawing at the crust, which crumbles it.
steps.fix: Use one long sharp stroke per cut.

science: Frenching is cosmetic, but trimming the fat cap matters for cooking: a thin cap renders and bastes the meat, while thick fat insulates it. Searing first browns the fat by the Maillard reaction; the crumb then goes on the cooled rack so it sticks to the mustard rather than sliding on hot fat. Lamb's muscle fibres are fine and tender, and keeping it below 135°F (57°C) keeps the proteins from contracting. For pommes Anna, unrinsed potato starch gelatinises in the hot butter and glues the slices into a cake. Clarified butter has had its water and milk solids removed, so it reaches higher temperatures without burning, browning the cake evenly and crisply.
plating: Set a wedge of pommes Anna at the back of a warm plate, spiral side up. Lean two double cutlets against it, bones crossed and pointing up, the pink cut faces and green crust showing. A spoonful of the lamb jus goes on the plate, and a sprig of thyme or a few leaves of watercress add colour.

pairing.drink: A Pauillac or a mature Rioja Reserva: Cabernet's cassis and cedar is the classic match for lamb, and its tannin cuts through the butter of the potatoes.
pairing.brennans: Château Haut-Bages Libéral Pauillac 5ème Cru Classé 2018: a Pauillac from the Brennan's list, the classic Bordeaux partner for pink lamb.

variations: Use a pistachio crust in place of the breadcrumbs.
Serve with a white bean and rosemary purée in place of the pommes Anna.
Make pommes boulangère in place of Anna, with the potatoes layered with onions and stock.
safety: Food safety guidance for whole cuts of lamb is 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest; medium-rare at 130°F (54°C) is a common choice for a rack.
Always use the mandoline guard; potatoes slip, and mandoline cuts are deep.
Turning out a hot pan: use oven gloves on both hands and turn away from you.

title: Coniglio alla Ligure
summary: Ligurian rabbit: a whole rabbit you joint into eight, browned in olive oil with garlic, rosemary and bay, cooked down with Vermentino and stock a ladle at a time, and finished with Taggiasca olives and pine nuts. It is in the course because breaking down a whole animal is a Chef's skill, and because the sauce is made by reduction alone, no flour, no cream.
skills: braising with wine, olives, pine nuts and herbs
equipment: Heavy cleaver and a sharp boning knife
Wide, heavy sauté pan or casserole with a lid, 12 inch (30 cm)
Small saucepan to keep stock hot
Ladle, tongs and a wooden spoon

ingredients.note: liver and kidneys kept aside if you like

ingredients.item: Vermentino or other dry white wine
Taggiasca olives in brine, stones in

mise: Pat the rabbit dry; remove any kidney fat and the thin membranes.
Heat the stock in the small saucepan and keep it at a simmer.
Drain the olives.

timeline.do: Joint the rabbit into 8; salt the pieces.
Brown the joints with garlic and herbs (15 minutes).
Add wine and cook it off; add stock a ladle at a time (45 minutes).
Add olives and pine nuts.
Let the last liquid go; swirl the pan to glaze.
Serve.

steps.do: Lay the rabbit on its back. Remove the front legs by cutting through the thin flesh under the shoulder blade: they are not attached by a joint, so they lift away. Then cut through the hip joint on each side to remove the hind legs, bending each leg back to pop the ball joint and cutting round it.
steps.look: Two front legs and two hind legs, each with a clean cut and no shattered bone.
steps.mistake: Chopping through the leg bones with the cleaver, which leaves splinters.
steps.fix: Find the joints with your fingers and cut through the tendons and gristle with the knife tip; use the cleaver only on the spine.

steps.do: Cut away the thin belly flaps, then chop the saddle (the loin section) across the spine into three equal pieces with one firm stroke of the cleaver each. Cut the rib cage into one piece. You will have 8 pieces: 2 hind legs, 2 front legs, 3 saddle pieces and the ribs.
steps.look: Eight even pieces with clean cuts, the saddle pieces showing round eyes of loin.
steps.mistake: Several hesitant cleaver blows, which shatter the spine into splinters.
steps.fix: Position the cleaver, then strike once firmly; press down on the back of the blade if it sticks.

steps.do: Season the pieces with the salt. Heat the oil in the sauté pan over medium heat, add the rabbit with the garlic, rosemary and bay, and brown on all sides for 12 to 15 minutes, turning, until golden.
steps.look: Golden joints and a pan that smells of resin and toasted garlic rather than scorch.
steps.mistake: High heat that burns the garlic black while the rabbit is still pale.
steps.fix: Lift out the garlic if it browns too fast; add it back later.

steps.do: Pour in the wine and let it boil away completely, turning the joints, for about 5 minutes, until the pan is dry again and the meat is frying in oil.
steps.look: Steam rising, then the sound changing from bubbling back to frying as the pan dries.
steps.mistake: Adding the stock before the wine has cooked off, so the sauce tastes sharp.
steps.fix: Wait until the pan sizzles again.

steps.do: Add the pepper and one ladle of hot stock. Cook uncovered over medium-low heat, turning the joints, and add another ladle each time the pan runs nearly dry. Continue for about 45 minutes until the hind leg meat gives at the bone.
steps.look: A slowly reducing, glossy liquid that coats the joints; the meat pulling back from the bone at the leg end.
steps.mistake: Pouring in all the stock at once and boiling it, so the rabbit stews rather than glazes.
steps.fix: Add stock a ladle at a time; if the stock runs out before the meat is tender, use hot water.

steps.do: Check the hind legs: the thickest part should reach 160°F (71°C) and the meat should pull easily from the bone. Lift out the saddle pieces earlier if they are done first, and return them at the end.
steps.look: Tender leg meat; firm but moist saddle.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the lean saddle into dry threads while the legs finish.
steps.fix: Take the saddle out after 30 minutes and keep it warm, then return it for the last minutes.

steps.do: Stir in the olives and pine nuts for the final 10 minutes, leaving the olive stones in so they hold their shape. Tell the table the stones are there.
steps.look: Pine nuts turning pale gold; olives shiny and plump.
steps.mistake: Adding the olives at the start, so they lose their fruit and turn bitter.
steps.fix: Keep them to the last 10 minutes.

steps.do: Let the last of the liquid reduce until the joints fry in the oil once more, then take the pan off the heat and swirl until the oil and pan juices cling as a glaze. Scatter with parsley and serve.
steps.look: A glossy, clinging glaze with no pool of thin liquid in the pan.
steps.mistake: Leaving a watery sauce.
steps.fix: Reduce for a couple of minutes more, shaking the pan to coat the pieces.

science: Rabbit is lean, and its muscles differ: the saddle is tender and quick to cook, while the legs carry more connective tissue and need longer to soften. Adding stock a ladle at a time keeps the cooking liquid shallow and hot, so the meat braises gently while the liquid keeps reducing and concentrating gelatin and flavour, rather than diluting it. The final fry in oil emulsifies the reduced juices with the fat into a glaze. Cooking the wine off completely removes its harsh alcohol and leaves acidity and fruit. Olive stones keep the olives intact, and short cooking keeps their fruitiness. Pine nuts are rich in oil, which toasts quickly in the hot pan.
plating: Serve family style in the pan or on a warm platter, the joints arranged so each guest gets a leg and a piece of saddle, glazed and glistening, with the olives and pine nuts scattered over and a few rosemary sprigs tucked in. A bowl for the olive stones and bread for the juices go on the table.

pairing.drink: A Ligurian Vermentino or a Rossese di Dolceacqua: herbal, saline and fresh, matching the olives and rosemary of the Riviera.
pairing.brennans: Gaia ‘Wild Ferment’ Assyrtiko Santorini 2023: a saline, herbal white on the Brennan's list that matches the olive and rosemary just as a Vermentino would.

variations: Use chicken thighs and drumsticks, cooked to 165°F (74°C).
Add a handful of chopped fresh tomatoes with the stock.
Serve with a simple potato purée or with polenta.
safety: Cook rabbit to at least 160°F (71°C) in the thickest part of the leg; food safety guidance treats it like other game.
Cleavers need a stable board: put a damp cloth beneath it, keep your free hand flat and away, and strike once.
Wash hands, knives and board after handling raw rabbit.

title: Svíčková na Smetaně
summary: Czech svíčková na smetaně: beef larded with bacon, marinated in vinegar with root vegetables, braised slowly, then served in a sauce made by sieving those roots with the braising liquid and finishing it with cream, alongside steamed bread dumplings, cranberries and lemon. It is in the course because the sauce is thickened by vegetables alone and passed until velvet, and the dumplings are a dough skill of their own.
skills: puréeing and passing the sauce with cream
equipment: Larding needle or a thin boning knife
Large non-reactive bowl or container for marinating
Heavy casserole with a lid, 5 quart (5 litre)
Large wide pot for boiling dumplings
Stand mixer with dough hook, or a large bowl and wooden spoon
Clean tea towel and cling film
Strong cotton thread for slicing dumplings

ingredients.item: Beef rump or topside, in one piece
Smoked streaky bacon, cut into long strips 1/4 inch (6 mm) wide, chilled
Strong white bread flour, for the dumplings
Day-old white bread, cut into 1/2 inch (1 cm) cubes
Lemon slices and whole-berry cranberry sauce

mise: The day before, lard the beef and put it in the marinade with the roots (steps 1 and 2).
Toast the bread cubes in a dry pan or a 350°F (180°C) oven for 8 minutes until crisp.
Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C) on the day.

timeline.do: Lard the beef; marinate it with the roots, vinegar and spices in the fridge for 24 hours.
Brown the beef; sweat the roots; braise for 2 1/2 to 3 hours.
Make the dumpling dough; prove 1 hour; shape; prove 30 minutes.
Boil the dumplings 10 minutes a side.
Rest the beef; blend and sieve the sauce.
Balance with sugar and lemon; add cream; warm the slices.
Slice dumplings with thread; plate with cranberry, lemon and cream.

steps.do: Lard the beef: push the larding needle or a thin knife lengthways through the meat along the grain at 1 inch (2.5 cm) intervals, then push a cold bacon strip into each channel. Trim the ends flush.
steps.look: A joint studded with bacon strips running along the grain, visible at each end.
steps.mistake: Using warm bacon, which smears and will not go in.
steps.fix: Keep the strips in the freezer for 10 minutes before larding.

steps.do: Put the beef, carrot, celeriac, parsley root, onion, peppercorns, allspice, bay and thyme in the bowl. Bring the vinegar and water to a boil with 1 tsp (5 g) salt, cool it to room temperature, pour it over, cover and refrigerate for 24 hours, turning the beef once.
steps.look: Beef and vegetables mostly covered by the marinade, a sharp, spiced smell.
steps.mistake: Pouring the hot marinade on, which starts to cook the surface of the meat.
steps.fix: Cool it to below 70°F (21°C) first.

steps.do: Lift out the beef, pat dry and season with 1 tsp (5 g) salt. Strain the vegetables, keeping the liquid. Melt the butter in the casserole over medium-high heat and brown the beef on all sides for 8 to 10 minutes until deep bronze, then lift it out.
steps.look: A dark, evenly browned crust and browned butter in the pan.
steps.mistake: Browning wet meat, which steams and stays grey.
steps.fix: Dry it well and do not crowd the pan.

steps.do: Add the drained vegetables and cook over medium heat, stirring, for 10 minutes until their edges caramelise and the pan smells sweet.
steps.look: Golden vegetables and brown deposits on the base.
steps.mistake: Burning the base, which will make the sauce bitter.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of stock to lift the deposits.

steps.do: Return the beef with the spices, 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the marinade liquid and the stock, enough to come a third of the way up the beef. Cover and braise at 300°F (150°C) for 2 1/2 to 3 hours until a skewer slides in with no resistance.
steps.look: Tender meat that yields to a skewer, and very soft vegetables.
steps.mistake: Using too much marinade, which makes the sauce too sour.
steps.fix: Start with a little; you will balance acidity at the end.

steps.do: Make the dumpling dough: mix the flour, yeast and 1 tsp (5 g) salt, add the milk and egg and knead for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Knead in the toasted bread cubes, cover and prove for 1 hour in a warm place until doubled.
steps.look: A soft, smooth dough with cubes of bread evenly through it, risen to twice its size.
steps.mistake: A dough too wet to hold its shape.
steps.fix: Knead in a little more flour, a spoonful at a time.

steps.do: Divide the dough in two and shape each into a log 2 1/2 inches (6 cm) thick and 8 inches (20 cm) long. Cover and prove 30 minutes.
steps.look: Two smooth, plump logs, slightly puffed.
steps.mistake: Shaping thick logs that stay raw in the middle.
steps.fix: Keep them to 2 1/2 inches (6 cm) thick.

steps.do: Bring a wide pot of salted water to a gentle boil. Lower in the logs, cover and simmer for 10 minutes, turn them over and simmer 10 minutes more. Lift out, prick all over with a skewer to release steam, and cover with a towel.
steps.look: Dumplings swollen and firm, with a skewer coming out clean.
steps.mistake: Boiling them hard, which makes them heavy and split.
steps.fix: Keep the water at a gentle simmer; if they sink, they will still cook, just turn them.

steps.do: Lift the beef out to rest. Discard the bay leaves, then blend the vegetables with the braising liquid until smooth and push through the fine sieve, pressing hard until only dry fibre is left.
steps.look: A smooth, thick, orange-brown sauce with no fibres.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve, so the sauce is gritty.
steps.fix: Push through the sieve in batches with a ladle.

steps.do: Return the sauce to the pan and simmer. Add sugar and lemon juice a little at a time until it tastes bright and gently sweet-sour, then take it off the heat and stir in the cream.
steps.look: A smooth, pale caramel-coloured sauce, creamy and balanced.
steps.mistake: Boiling the sauce after adding the cream to an acidic base, which can curdle it.
steps.fix: Add the cream off the heat; if it does curdle, blend it again.

steps.do: Slice the beef across the grain into slices 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick and warm them in the sauce for 2 minutes. Slice the dumplings 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick by looping thread round them and pulling it tight.
steps.look: Clean dumpling slices that do not squash, and tender beef slices glazed with sauce.
steps.mistake: Slicing dumplings with a knife, which compresses them.
steps.fix: Use thread; a serrated knife used gently is a second choice.

steps.do: Plate the beef with four or five dumpling slices, plenty of sauce, a lemon slice topped with a spoonful of cranberry sauce and a dollop of whipped cream.
steps.look: Golden sauce, white dumplings and the bright red cranberry on lemon.
steps.mistake: Not enough sauce; the dumplings should be soaked in it.
steps.fix: Serve extra sauce at the table.

science: Svíčková's sauce is thickened by vegetable purée, not flour. Long braising softens the cell walls of the carrot, celeriac and parsley root, and blending releases pectin and starch, which hold water and give body. Sieving removes fibre so the sauce is smooth. The vinegar marinade does little to tenderise the meat inside, but it seasons and flavours the surface and gives the sauce its sour backbone. Braising at 300°F (150°C) keeps the liquid around 200°F (93°C), turning collagen in the beef into gelatin over hours. Cream added to an acidic sauce off the heat stays smooth, because boiling acid and dairy together makes casein proteins clump. Yeast in the dumplings makes gas that sets into a soft crumb as they boil.
plating: Use warm, wide plates. Lay two or three slices of beef slightly overlapping, with four or five dumpling slices fanned beside them. Ladle sauce generously over the beef and dumplings. Put a lemon slice at the top of the plate with a spoon of cranberry sauce and a small piped rosette of whipped cream on it.

pairing.drink: A Czech or Austrian lager, or a fruity Blaufränkisch: the beer's bitterness or the wine's bright acidity cut through the cream, and its fruit suits the cranberries.

variations: Use beef cheek or chuck, braised a little longer.
Serve with potato dumplings instead of bread dumplings.
Add a spoon of Dijon mustard to the sauce for extra bite.
safety: Marinate the beef in the fridge at or below 40°F (4°C), never on the counter.
Braised beef should reach at least 145°F (63°C); after 2 hours braising it will be far above this.
Lift the casserole lid away from you; trapped steam burns.
Cool leftover sauce and beef within 2 hours and refrigerate.

title: Matambre Arrollado
summary: Argentine matambre arrollado: a large, thin sheet of beef marinated in garlic, oregano and vinegar, laid with spinach, carrots, roasted peppers, olives and whole eggs, rolled tight, tied, poached, then pressed overnight and sliced cold into a mosaic. It is in the course because it tests butterflying, rolling and tying, and the patience of an overnight press.
skills: a filling of eggs, carrots and peppers
equipment: Muslin or a clean cotton cloth, or heavy foil
Large pot or roasting tin that fits the roll
Two baking trays and weights (tins) for pressing

ingredients.item: Flank steak (or matambre, if your butcher has it)
Carrots, cut into batons 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick and blanched 3 minutes
Beef or chicken stock, for poaching
Chimichurri: parsley, oregano, garlic, vinegar, olive oil, chilli

mise: Hard-boil the eggs for 10 minutes and cool in iced water.
Blanch the carrot batons in boiling salted water for 3 minutes, then cool.
Roast the peppers until black, sweat in a bowl under film, peel and cut into strips.

timeline.do: Butterfly, marinate 2 hours, fill, roll, tie and poach; press overnight.
Make the chimichurri.
Take the roll from the press; slice.
Serve cold or at room temperature with chimichurri.

steps.do: Lay the flank steak on the board with the grain running left to right. With the long knife held parallel to the board, cut into one long side, halfway up the thickness, and open the steak like a book, cutting to within 1/2 inch (1 cm) of the far edge.
steps.look: One wide, thin sheet about twice the original width.
steps.mistake: Cutting all the way through.
steps.fix: If you do, overlap the two pieces by 1 inch (2.5 cm) and they will hold when rolled.

steps.do: Cover the sheet with cling film and pound it with the mallet to an even 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.look: An even, rectangular sheet with no thick spots.
steps.mistake: Pounding too hard and tearing it.
steps.fix: Use firm, even strokes; patch tears with the filling.

steps.do: Mix the garlic, oregano, chilli, vinegar, 1 tsp (5 g) salt and pepper and rub over the meat. Cover and marinate in the fridge for 2 hours.
steps.look: Meat coated and fragrant with garlic and oregano.
steps.mistake: Marinating overnight in vinegar, which turns the meat mushy at the surface.
steps.fix: Keep to 2 to 4 hours.

steps.do: Lay the sheet with the grain running away from you, so you will roll across the grain. Cover with spinach, leaving a 1 inch (2.5 cm) border at the far end. Lay carrots, peppers and olives in lanes running across the sheet, parallel to the edge you will roll from. Lay the eggs end to end in a line one third of the way in.
steps.look: Neat, tight lanes of colour running across the sheet.
steps.mistake: Running the lanes in the rolling direction, so every slice shows the same colour.
steps.fix: Lay them across; each slice will show all the colours.

steps.do: Roll tightly from the near edge, tucking the filling in as you go, finishing seam side down. Tie with twine every 1 1/2 inches (4 cm), then tie once lengthways.
steps.look: A tight, even cylinder about 4 inches (10 cm) across.
steps.mistake: A loose roll that slips when poached.
steps.fix: Re-roll more tightly, pressing as you go; tie firmly.

steps.do: Wrap the roll tightly in a 20 inch (50 cm) square of muslin or two layers of heavy foil, twisting and tying the ends so it keeps its round shape.
steps.look: A firm, sealed parcel.
steps.mistake: Loose wrapping, so the roll swells and loses shape.
steps.fix: Twist the ends tightly and tie with twine.

steps.do: Lower the roll into the stock, bring to a bare simmer and cook for 1 1/2 hours, turning once, until a skewer slides easily into the meat and the centre reads 165°F (74°C) or higher.
steps.look: A gentle simmer with occasional bubbles, and a tender roll.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which toughens the meat.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low; small bubbles only.

steps.do: Lift the roll out, still wrapped, onto a tray. Put a second tray on top and weight it with tins. Cool for 30 minutes, then refrigerate overnight under the weight.
steps.look: A slightly flattened roll that holds its shape and is firm and cold.
steps.mistake: Skipping the press, so the slices crumble.
steps.fix: Press for at least 6 hours; overnight is best.

steps.do: Unwrap, snip off the twine, and cut into slices 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick with the long knife. Serve cold or at room temperature with chimichurri.
steps.look: A mosaic of red meat, green spinach, orange carrot, red pepper and yellow egg in every slice.
steps.mistake: Cutting thin slices that fall apart.
steps.fix: Keep slices at least 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick and use a long, sharp knife.

science: Flank steak is a thin, hard-working muscle with long fibres. Rolling it across the grain means each slice cuts the fibres short, making it tender to eat. Poaching gently around 190°F (88°C) for 90 minutes converts collagen to gelatin without driving all the moisture out. Pressing while it cools sets that gelatin and fat in place, gluing the filling and meat together, so the roll slices cleanly into a mosaic rather than crumbling. Vinegar in the marinade adds sharp flavour to the surface, but long contact with acid would break down the surface proteins into a mushy layer. The hard-boiled eggs and carrots are cooked before rolling, so they need only heating through.
plating: Lay four or five slices overlapping on a long board or platter, cut face up to show the mosaic. Spoon chimichurri in a line beside them, not over them, and serve with crusty bread.

pairing.drink: An Argentine Malbec: its plum fruit and soft tannin suit cold beef, and its acidity handles the vinegar in the chimichurri.

variations: Add strips of ham or bacon among the filling.
Roast the roll in the oven, covered with stock, at 325°F (160°C) for 1 1/2 hours.
Serve warm in thick slices with a tomato sauce.
safety: Stuffed rolled meat should reach 165°F (74°C) in the centre, because the inside surface was handled raw.
Cool the cooked roll quickly in the fridge and keep it at or below 40°F (4°C); eat within 3 days.
Keep raw meat away from the cooked eggs and vegetables until rolling.

title: Jerk Chicken over Pimento Wood
summary: Jamaican jerk chicken as it should be: quarters slashed to the bone, marinated overnight in a scotch bonnet, allspice and spring onion paste, and cooked slowly over coals with pimento wood smoke, then chopped with a cleaver. It is here because jerk is a fire technique, not a spice mix: smoke, indirect heat and patience over a lidded fire.
skills: a Scotch bonnet and allspice marinade
equipment: Kettle grill with a lid, charcoal and a chimney starter (or a gas grill set for indirect heat)
Pimento (allspice) wood chunks or chips, or 1/2 cup (60 g) whole allspice berries soaked in water
Large zip bags or a non-reactive dish

ingredients.note: seeds in for heat, out for less

ingredients.item: Whole allspice berries, toasted and ground
Rice and peas, and lime wedges

mise: Wear gloves to handle the scotch bonnets.
Toast the allspice berries in a dry pan for 2 minutes until fragrant, then grind.
Soak the pimento wood chips or allspice berries in water for 30 minutes.

timeline.do: Make the paste; slash and marinate the chicken overnight.
Light the charcoal; set up for indirect heat.
Put the chicken on; cook lid down, turning every 10 minutes.
Add pimento wood or allspice berries to the coals.
Char the skin over the coals; check temperature; rest.
Chop with the cleaver and serve with rice and peas.

steps.do: Blend the scotch bonnets, spring onions, garlic, ginger, thyme, allspice, cinnamon, nutmeg, pepper, sugar, soy, lime, oil and salt to a thick paste.
steps.look: A thick, green-brown paste with an intense, fiery, spiced smell.
steps.mistake: Breathing over the blender, which catches your throat.
steps.fix: Open it away from your face and keep the kitchen ventilated.

steps.do: Slash each chicken quarter to the bone 3 or 4 times, 1 inch (2.5 cm) apart. Rub the paste into the slashes and all over, under the skin where you can. Seal in bags and refrigerate overnight, at least 12 hours.
steps.look: Chicken coated deep green, the paste pushed into every cut.
steps.mistake: Marinating only an hour, so the flavour stays on the surface.
steps.fix: Marinate overnight; jerk seasons to the bone.

steps.do: Light a full chimney of charcoal. When covered in grey ash, pour the coals to one side of the grill, leaving the other side empty. Set the grate on, cover and heat until the lid thermometer reads 300 to 325°F (150 to 160°C).
steps.look: A steady, moderate heat with a hot side and a cool side.
steps.mistake: Putting the chicken over direct coals for the whole time, which burns the outside before the inside cooks.
steps.fix: Use the cool side for most of the cooking.

steps.do: Lay the chicken skin side up on the cool side, close the lid with its vent above the chicken, and cook for 40 to 50 minutes, turning and swapping the pieces every 10 minutes.
steps.look: The skin darkening slowly; smoke drifting from the vent.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid too often, which loses heat and smoke.
steps.fix: Open only to turn; keep the lid on otherwise.

steps.do: For the last 20 minutes, scatter the drained pimento chips or allspice berries over the coals so they smoke.
steps.look: A sweet, clove-like, peppery smoke rising.
steps.mistake: Adding dry chips that flame instead of smoke.
steps.fix: Soak them well first.

steps.do: Move the chicken over the coals for the last 5 minutes and char the skin, turning, until blackened in places. Check the thighs reach 175°F (79°C) and the breasts 165°F (74°C).
steps.look: Crisp, charred skin and clear juices.
steps.mistake: Leaving the breast over the coals as long as the legs, so it dries out.
steps.fix: Take the breast off first; the leg can stay longer.

steps.do: Rest for 5 minutes, then chop through the bone with the cleaver into pieces 2 inches (5 cm) wide, and serve with rice and peas and lime wedges.
steps.look: Juicy pieces with a red smoke ring under charred skin.
steps.mistake: Chopping hesitantly, which splinters the bone.
steps.fix: One firm stroke per cut.

science: Smoke flavour comes from wood burning at low temperatures, which releases aromatic compounds; pimento wood brings the clove-like eugenol also found in allspice berries. Indirect heat cooks the chicken slowly, so the collagen in the legs softens and the meat stays moist, while the lid keeps smoke circulating. Slashing to the bone increases the surface for the paste, and an overnight marinade lets salt penetrate deeply, seasoning and helping the meat hold moisture. Scotch bonnets contain capsaicin, which dissolves in fat, so the heat spreads through the oily paste. Brown sugar caramelises when the skin is charred over direct heat at the end, giving the dark, sticky crust.
plating: Pile the chopped pieces on a board or platter, charred skin up, with a mound of rice and peas beside them and lime wedges. Serve with hard dough bread and a small bowl of extra jerk paste or hot pepper sauce.

pairing.drink: A Red Stripe lager, or an off-dry Riesling or Gewurztraminer: cold beer or a little sweetness cools the scotch bonnet, and the aromatic wine meets the allspice.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives 2007: a rich, aromatic Alsace wine from the Brennan's list whose sweetness and spice tame scotch bonnet heat.

variations: Jerk pork shoulder, cooked slowly to 195°F (90°C) and chopped.
Use chicken wings, cooked 25 to 30 minutes.
Cook in the oven at 350°F (180°C) for 45 minutes and finish under a hot overhead grill (broiler) if you cannot cook outside, adding smoked paprika to the paste.
safety: Cook chicken to 165°F (74°C) in the breast; thighs are better at 175°F (79°C).
Wear gloves for scotch bonnets and never touch your eyes; wash hands and board well.
Grill outdoors only and keep a safe distance from buildings; let coals cool fully before disposal.
Use separate tongs for raw and cooked chicken.

title: Siu Yuk (Cantonese Crackling Pork Belly)
summary: Cantonese siu yuk: a slab of pork belly with skin blanched, pricked, dried overnight and roasted under a salt crust, then blasted until it puffs into crackling as light as glass over juicy, spiced meat. It is here because crackling of this standard is a lesson in controlling water: every step either dries the skin or protects it.
skills: blanching and pricking the skin all over
equipment: Meat pricker, or a cluster of 4 to 6 cocktail sticks or a sharp skewer

ingredients.item: Pork belly, skin on, boneless, in one even slab
Fine sea salt, for the meat
Fermented red bean curd (naam yu), mashed
Coarse rock salt, for the crust
Dijon or English mustard, or hoisin, to serve

mise: Clear a flat shelf in the fridge for the pork to dry uncovered overnight.
Mix the salt, sugar, five spice, white pepper, naam yu and wine into a paste.

timeline.do: Blanch, prick, season the meat side and dry uncovered in the fridge for 24 hours.
Oven to 400°F (200°C); wrap in foil and pack the salt crust.
Roast under salt 40 minutes.
Remove the crust; raise the oven to 475°F (250°C); blast 15 to 25 minutes.
Rest 15 minutes.
Chop skin side down with a cleaver and serve with mustard.

steps.do: Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Hold the belly skin side down in the water for 3 to 4 minutes, keeping the meat out, until the skin turns from soft and waxy to firm and matte. Dry it well.
steps.look: Skin firm and pale, contracted slightly.
steps.mistake: Submerging the whole slab, which partly cooks the meat.
steps.fix: Hold only the skin in the water with tongs, or ladle boiling water over the skin.

steps.do: While still warm, prick the skin all over with the pricker or cocktail sticks, densely, about 40 to 50 holes per square inch (6 per square centimetre), through the skin but not into the meat.
steps.look: A dense, even field of small holes across the whole skin.
steps.mistake: Pricking into the fat and meat, so juices bubble up and wet the skin.
steps.fix: Keep the points shallow; press just through the skin.

steps.do: Turn the belly over and score the meat side 1/2 inch (1 cm) deep at 1 inch (2.5 cm) intervals. Rub the seasoning paste into the meat and the sides only, keeping every trace off the skin.
steps.look: Meat coated red-brown, the skin completely clean.
steps.mistake: Getting seasoning on the skin, which burns and stops it puffing.
steps.fix: Wipe the skin clean with a damp cloth, then dry it.

steps.do: Set the belly skin side up on the rack over the tray and refrigerate uncovered for 24 hours.
steps.look: Skin dry, tight and feeling like parchment.
steps.mistake: Covering it, which keeps the skin moist.
steps.fix: Leave it open; if your fridge is humid, dab the skin with paper and dry it longer.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Brush the skin with the vinegar. Wrap the meat sides in a tight foil boat so only the skin is exposed, with the foil walls rising 1/2 inch (1 cm) above the skin.
steps.look: A neat foil tray hugging the meat, skin exposed and glistening with vinegar.
steps.mistake: Gaps in the foil, so the salt touches the meat.
steps.fix: Fold the foil corners tightly and press it to the sides of the belly.

steps.do: Mix the rock salt with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and pack it over the skin in an even layer 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick. Roast for 40 minutes.
steps.look: The salt hardening into a crust.
steps.mistake: A thin salt layer that cracks and lets the skin brown unevenly.
steps.fix: Pack it firmly and evenly.

steps.do: Lift off the salt crust in one piece and brush away the grains. Raise the oven to 475°F (250°C) and roast the belly, skin up, for 15 to 25 minutes, turning the tray every 5 minutes, until the whole skin has puffed into tiny bubbles and is golden. The meat should reach at least 190°F (88°C).
steps.look: Crackling puffing into blistered foam, crackling sounds from the oven, and a hollow ring when tapped.
steps.mistake: Leaving it until the skin burns black in patches.
steps.fix: Watch closely; cover any blackening patch with a piece of foil and continue for the rest.

steps.do: Rest for 15 minutes, skin side up and uncovered, on the rack so that air circulates underneath and the base stays crisp.
steps.look: The crackling hardens as it cools.
steps.mistake: Covering it with foil, which steams the crackling soft.
steps.fix: Never cover it.

steps.do: Turn the belly skin side down on the board and chop with a heavy cleaver into pieces 1 by 1 1/2 inches (2.5 by 4 cm), using one firm stroke each. Serve with mustard or hoisin.
steps.look: Neat pieces with a layer of crackling, white fat and pink-brown meat.
steps.mistake: Cutting skin side up, which shatters the crackling.
steps.fix: Always cut skin side down, pressing through in one stroke.

science: Crackling is skin dried so far that its remaining water flashes into steam and puffs the softened collagen into a crisp foam. Blanching contracts and partly cooks the skin, and pricking makes holes for steam and fat to escape. Drying uncovered for a day evaporates water, and vinegar's acid helps break down surface proteins and evaporates quickly. The salt crust absorbs moisture while the meat roasts, and keeps the skin from overheating before the fat beneath renders. When the crust comes off, the high heat makes the dried, rendered skin blister and puff. Belly's fat and collagen need long heat to soften, which is why the meat is cooked far above the minimum safe temperature.
plating: Arrange the pieces on a plate or board in neat rows, crackling up, slightly fanned so the three layers show. Serve with a small dish of mustard and some plain rice or steamed greens with oyster sauce.

pairing.drink: A Pinot Noir from Burgundy or Oregon, or a dry sparkling wine: Pinot's bright acidity and soft tannin cut the fat, while bubbles scrub the palate after every rich bite.
pairing.brennans: Bergstrom ‘Reserve’ Pinot Noir Willamette Valley 2022 (375 ml): a bright Oregon Pinot on the Brennan's list with acidity to cut through the rich belly.

variations: Add a thin layer of hoisin and maltose to the meat for a char siu flavour.
Cook a smaller slab and serve it over rice with steamed bok choy.
Use the same drying method for a British roast pork with crackling.
safety: Pork is safe at 145°F (63°C), but belly needs 190°F (88°C) or more to become tender.
Store the drying pork on the bottom shelf, away from ready-to-eat food.
Blasting at 475°F (250°C) spits fat: use oven gloves, and open the door slowly.
A cleaver needs a stable board: put a damp cloth under it and keep your guiding hand clear.

title: Steak and Kidney Pudding
summary: The great British steamed pudding: a basin lined with soft suet pastry, packed with beef and ox kidney braised in stout, sealed with a pastry lid and steamed for hours until the crust is light and the gravy dark. It is here because suet pastry, careful offal preparation and long, steady steaming are three skills the trade rarely drills.
skills: a raw filling of beef and trimmed kidney
equipment: Large pot with lid that the basin fits in, with an upturned saucer or trivet on the base
Large bowl and a rolling pin
Kettle for topping up boiling water

ingredients.item: Beef chuck, in 1 inch (2.5 cm) dice
Plain flour, seasoned with salt and pepper

mise: Soak the kidney in cold salted water for 30 minutes, then cut out every trace of the white core and tubes.
Butter the basin.
Cut a circle of parchment and foil 4 inches (10 cm) wider than the top of the basin and fold a pleat in the middle of both together.

timeline.do: Prepare the kidney; brown the meat; braise the filling 1 1/2 hours; cool.
Make the suet pastry; line the basin; fill and seal.
Steam for 4 hours, topping up with boiling water.
Lift out and rest.
Turn out and serve with greens.

steps.do: Pat the cored kidney dry. Toss the beef and kidney in the seasoned flour. Heat the dripping in the heavy pan over high heat and brown the meat in batches for 3 to 4 minutes each until dark on all sides.
steps.look: Deep brown crust on the meat, and brown deposits in the pan.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan, so the meat steams grey.
steps.fix: Brown in two or three batches.

steps.do: Soften the onion in the same pan for 5 minutes, then return the meat and add the stout, stock, Worcestershire, thyme and bay. Simmer gently, covered, for 1 1/2 hours until the beef is nearly tender. Cool completely.
steps.look: Thick, dark, glossy gravy and beef that gives to a fork.
steps.mistake: Filling the pastry with hot filling, which melts the suet.
steps.fix: Cool to room temperature, or chill it.

steps.do: Make the pastry: mix the self-raising flour, suet and salt, then add about 2/3 cup (150 ml) cold water a little at a time, mixing with a knife, until it forms a soft dough. Bring together with as little handling as possible.
steps.look: A soft, slightly sticky dough that holds together.
steps.mistake: Kneading it, which makes a tough crust.
steps.fix: Bring it together quickly and stop.

steps.do: Cut off one quarter for the lid. Roll the rest into a circle 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick and large enough to line the basin. Lower it in and press it to the sides, leaving an overhang.
steps.look: An even pastry lining with no thin spots or holes.
steps.mistake: Thin spots that tear and let the gravy out.
steps.fix: Patch any thin spots with trimmings, pressed with wet fingers.

steps.do: Pack in the cold filling with enough gravy to come three-quarters up, keeping the rest to serve. Roll the lid, brush the lining's edge with water, lay the lid on and press to seal; trim.
steps.look: A sealed pudding with the filling below the rim.
steps.mistake: Overfilling with gravy, which bursts the seal.
steps.fix: Leave a little space; keep extra gravy for serving.

steps.do: Cover with the pleated parchment and foil, tie string tightly under the rim with 2 turns, and make a string handle over the top about 6 inches (15 cm) long.
steps.look: A neat, sealed cover with room to expand.
steps.mistake: Covering without a pleat, so the pudding pushes the cover off as it rises.
steps.fix: Always fold a pleat.

steps.do: Set the basin on the trivet in the pot, pour boiling water to come halfway up the basin, cover and steam over low heat for 4 hours, topping up with boiling water every 45 minutes.
steps.look: A steady simmer and steam rising round the lid.
steps.mistake: Letting the pot boil dry, or topping up with cold water, which drops the temperature and makes the crust heavy.
steps.fix: Set a timer and always top up with water from a just-boiled kettle.

steps.do: Lift out the basin by the string, rest 10 minutes, then remove the cover, run a knife round the edge and turn out onto a warm plate.
steps.look: A pale golden dome, steaming and firm.
steps.mistake: Turning out at once, so it collapses.
steps.fix: Rest it first so the crust firms.

steps.do: Cut into 4 wedges at the table, letting the gravy flow out, and serve with about 1/2 cup (120 ml) extra hot gravy each, greens and mashed potato.
steps.look: A light crust and rich, dark filling.
steps.mistake: Serving cold gravy.
steps.fix: Heat the reserved gravy until bubbling.

science: Suet is hard beef fat that melts at a higher temperature than butter, around 113°F (45°C). The crust sets around the solid flecks of suet before they melt, and as they melt, the fat coats the flour and the steam trapped in the dough lifts it, giving a light, soft crust without lamination. Self-raising flour adds a little chemical lift. Long steaming keeps the temperature steady at 212°F (100°C), so the crust cooks through without browning. Kidneys contain urea; soaking and removing the white core and tubes takes away the ammonia taste. Browning the floured meat develops Maillard flavours, and the flour thickens the stout gravy.
plating: Bring the whole pudding to the table on a warm plate. Cut a wedge and lift it out onto a warm plate so the dark gravy and meat flow out of the pale crust. Serve with buttered greens, mash and a jug of extra gravy.

pairing.drink: A glass of the same stout, or a Rhône red: stout echoes the gravy's dark malt, and a Syrah-Grenache blend has the depth and spice for offal.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de Châteaumar ‘Cuvée Vincent’ Côtes du Rhône 2023: a generous Rhône red on the Brennan's list with the depth and spice for beef, kidney and stout.

variations: Steak and mushroom pudding: replace the kidney with chestnut mushrooms.
Add oysters to the filling, as in Victorian puddings.
Bake the filling under a puff pastry lid for a steak and kidney pie.
safety: Beef and kidney must reach at least 160°F (71°C); after 4 hours of steaming they will be far above this.
Lift the basin out with oven gloves and the string handle; steam burns.
Cool and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

title: Javaher Polow (Jewelled Rice) with Saffron Chicken
summary: Persian jewelled rice: long-grain basmati parboiled in brine, steamed over a golden tahdig crust and studded with candied orange peel, carrot, barberries, pistachios and almonds, served with saffron-braised chicken. It is in the course because Persian rice is a discipline of its own, where the moment you drain, the steam and the crust decide everything.
skills: parboiling and steaming rice with tahdig
equipment: Heavy non-stick pot with a tight lid, 10 inch (25 cm) wide
Large pot for parboiling the rice
Clean tea towel to wrap the lid
Medium frying pan and a small saucepan
Heavy casserole with lid for the chicken

ingredients.item: Fine salt, for soaking and parboiling
Caster sugar, for grinding with saffron
Orange peel, pith removed, in fine strips
Advieh (Persian rice spice) or ground cinnamon

mise: Rinse the rice in cool water five or six times until the water runs nearly clear, then soak it in cold water with 2 tbsp (35 g) of the salt for 1 to 2 hours.
Grind the saffron with 1 tsp (4 g) sugar in the mortar to a fine powder, add the hot water and leave 20 minutes.
Blanch the orange peel strips in boiling water for 1 minute three times, changing the water, to remove bitterness.

timeline.do: Rinse and soak the rice; bloom the saffron; blanch the peel.
Braise the saffron chicken (about 1 hour).
Candy the orange peel and carrots; plump the barberries.
Parboil the rice; build the tahdig; steam 50 minutes.
Toast the nuts; warm the barberries.
Spoon out the rice, layer with jewels and turn out the tahdig.

steps.do: Fry the onions in 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil in the casserole over medium heat for 15 minutes until deep golden. Add the turmeric and pepper for 30 seconds, then the chicken, 1 tsp (5 g) salt and half the saffron water. Cover and cook over low heat for 45 to 60 minutes, turning once, until the meat slides off the bone.
steps.look: Golden onions, a fragrant yellow sauce, chicken tender to a spoon.
steps.mistake: Burning the onions, which turns the sauce bitter.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of water to stop the browning.

steps.do: Candy the jewels: put the blanched orange peel and carrots in the saucepan with the 1/4 cup (50 g) sugar and 1/2 cup (120 ml) water. Simmer 8 to 10 minutes until the liquid becomes a light syrup and the carrots are tender. Drain, keeping the syrup.
steps.look: Translucent, glossy orange strips and bright carrot matchsticks.
steps.mistake: Boiling until it caramelises, which makes them hard and brown.
steps.fix: Keep it at a simmer and stop at a light syrup.

steps.do: Bring 12 cups (3 litres) water to a fierce boil with the remaining salt. Drain the soaked rice and add it to the boiling water. Boil for 5 to 7 minutes, stirring gently once, until a grain bends between your fingers without snapping but still has a firm, chalky core when bitten.
steps.look: Grains doubled in length, rising to the surface, with a slight chalky centre.
steps.mistake: Boiling until soft right through, which turns the rice to mush during steaming.
steps.fix: Start testing at 4 minutes; drain the moment the core is still firm.

steps.do: Drain the rice in the sieve and rinse briefly with lukewarm water to stop it cooking and remove surface salt.
steps.look: Separate grains with no starchy film.
steps.mistake: Leaving it in the hot water while you find the sieve.
steps.fix: Have the sieve ready in the sink before the rice goes in.

steps.do: Make the tahdig: put 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil and 2 tbsp (30 g) butter in the clean non-stick pot over medium heat. Mix 2 cups (about 300 g) of the drained rice with the yoghurt and 2 tbsp (30 ml) saffron water and spread it evenly over the base, pressing down firmly.
steps.look: An even, yellow layer about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick, sizzling quietly.
steps.mistake: Making the layer too thick, so it never crisps.
steps.fix: Keep it to 1/2 inch (1 cm).

steps.do: Spoon the rest of the rice over in a cone, scattering a little cardamom and advieh between the layers. Poke 5 holes to the base with the handle of a wooden spoon. Drizzle 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and the remaining butter, melted, over the top.
steps.look: A neat cone of rice with steam holes.
steps.mistake: Pressing the rice down, which compacts it.
steps.fix: Spoon it loosely; height lets the steam circulate.

steps.do: Wrap the lid in a tea towel, tie the corners on top, and cover the pot tightly. Cook on medium for 10 minutes until steam is visible round the lid, then turn the heat to its lowest for 45 to 50 minutes.
steps.look: Steam escaping, and a toasty smell after 30 minutes.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid, which lets the steam escape.
steps.fix: Leave it closed; trust the smell of toasting rice.

steps.do: Plump the barberries: soak them in cold water for 10 minutes, drain, then warm them in 1 tbsp (15 g) butter with 1 tbsp (12 g) sugar for 1 minute until glossy and plump. Toast the nuts in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant.
steps.look: Glossy, red barberries and lightly golden nuts.
steps.mistake: Cooking barberries more than a minute, so they burn and turn bitter.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low and take them off quickly.

steps.do: Spoon the rice onto a platter in layers with the candied peel, carrots, barberries and nuts, drizzling a little saffron water over parts so they turn golden. Turn out the tahdig by placing a plate over the pot and flipping it, or break it into pieces to arrange around the rice.
steps.look: Fluffy, separate grains, yellow and white, studded with jewels, and a crisp golden crust.
steps.mistake: Stirring the jewels through, which crushes the grains.
steps.fix: Layer gently with a spoon.

steps.do: Lift the chicken onto the platter beside the rice and spoon over its sauce. Drizzle the reserved candying syrup lightly over the rice with the lemon juice.
steps.look: A bright, glossy chicken and a jewelled mound of rice.
steps.mistake: Pouring the chicken sauce over the rice, making it soggy.
steps.fix: Serve the sauce in a bowl.

science: Persian rice depends on controlling starch and water. Soaking hydrates the grains so they cook evenly and lengthen. Boiling in heavily salted water seasons the grains, since rice absorbs salt only while boiling. Draining while the core is still chalky leaves just enough raw starch to finish cooking in the steam without bursting. The lid wrapped in a cloth absorbs condensation so water does not drip back and turn the rice soggy. The tahdig crisps because the yoghurt and rice at the base, in contact with hot fat, undergo Maillard browning. Saffron's colour comes from crocin, which dissolves in water, and its aroma from safranal, released by grinding and gentle heat.
plating: On a large warm platter, build a broad mound of rice, the white and gold parts showing, and scatter the jewels in a band over the top: orange, red barberries, green pistachios and white almonds. Break the tahdig into large shards and stand them round the edge. Set the saffron chicken alongside or in a separate dish.

pairing.drink: A dry, aromatic white such as Condrieu Viognier or an Alsace Pinot Gris: apricot and floral notes meet saffron and orange, and the texture suits the buttered rice.
pairing.brennans: André Perret Condrieu 2019: a Viognier on the Brennan's list with apricot and floral notes that sing with saffron and orange peel.

variations: Zereshk polow: use only barberries and saffron, with no other jewels.
Make a potato tahdig by laying thin slices of potato on the base instead of rice and yoghurt.
Serve with lamb shanks braised with saffron instead of chicken.
safety: Cook chicken to 165°F (74°C); braised thighs will be far beyond this.
Cool leftover rice within an hour and refrigerate, as cooked rice left warm can grow bacteria; reheat until steaming.
Flipping the hot pot: use oven gloves and a plate larger than the pot, and turn away from you.

title: Dum Pukht Raan (Slow-Cooked Leg of Lamb)
summary: An Awadhi leg of lamb, scored to the bone, marinated overnight in yoghurt, raw papaya, ginger, garlic and fried onion with warm spices, then sealed in a pot under dough and cooked slowly in its own steam until it falls from the bone. It is here because dum, sealed slow cooking, is the technique of the Lucknow kitchens and it rewards trust: you cannot look inside.
skills: trimming and piercing a whole leg
equipment: Boning knife and a sharp chef's knife
Large heavy casserole with a tight lid, large enough for the leg
Large non-reactive dish or bag for marinating
Small bowl and rolling pin for the sealing dough

ingredients.item: Half leg of lamb (shank end), bone in
Raw green papaya, peeled and grated (or 1 tbsp (15 g) meat tenderiser)
Saffron, steeped in 2 tbsp (30 ml) warm milk
Mint and coriander leaves, red onion rings and lime

mise: Trim the papery skin (fell) and any thick fat off the lamb.
Slice the onions thinly and evenly so they fry evenly.

timeline.do: Score the lamb; fry birista onions; marinate overnight.
Take the lamb out of the fridge; oven to 325°F (160°C).
Seal the pot with dough; dum in the oven 3 hours.
Break the seal; check tenderness; reduce sauce if needed.
Serve with naan, onions and mint.

steps.do: Trim the fell (the thin papery membrane) and any fat thicker than 1/8 inch (3 mm) off the leg. Make deep cuts 1 inch (2.5 cm) apart all over, down to the bone, and prick between the cuts with a knife tip.
steps.look: Deep, even slashes all round the leg, exposing the meat to the bone.
steps.mistake: Shallow cuts that leave the marinade on the surface.
steps.fix: Cut down until you feel the bone.

steps.do: Fry the onions in the ghee over medium heat for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring, until deep golden brown and crisp. Lift out onto paper and keep the ghee.
steps.look: Crisp, mahogany onions and a sweet, nutty smell.
steps.mistake: Burning the onions, which turns the dish bitter.
steps.fix: Take them out when golden brown; they darken more as they cool.

steps.do: Blend the fried onions, yoghurt, ginger-garlic paste, papaya, chilli, garam masala, cumin, coriander, mace, salt and lemon juice to a smooth, thick marinade.
steps.look: A thick, brown paste with a rich, spiced smell.
steps.mistake: Adding too much lemon, which can curdle the yoghurt.
steps.fix: Stir in a spoon more yoghurt to smooth it.

steps.do: Rub the marinade deep into every cut and all over the lamb. Cover and refrigerate for 12 to 24 hours.
steps.look: The leg completely coated, marinade pushed into the slashes.
steps.mistake: Marinating longer than 24 hours with papaya, which turns the surface mushy.
steps.fix: Keep to 12 to 24 hours.

steps.do: Take the lamb out an hour before cooking. Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C). Mix the flour and water into a soft dough and roll it into a rope 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick.
steps.look: A pliable rope of dough long enough to go round the rim of the pot.
steps.mistake: A dry, crumbly dough that cracks.
steps.fix: Add more water a teaspoon at a time.

steps.do: Put 3 tbsp (45 g) of the onion ghee in the casserole, lay the lamb in with all the marinade, the cardamom and the saffron milk. Press the dough rope round the rim, set the lid on and press down to seal.
steps.look: A tight seal of dough all round the lid.
steps.mistake: Gaps in the seal, so steam escapes and the meat dries.
steps.fix: Patch any gaps with more dough.

steps.do: Cook on the middle shelf of the 325°F (160°C) oven for 3 hours, without opening the pot or disturbing the seal at any point.
steps.look: A seal that has hardened and browned; the kitchen smells of spice.
steps.mistake: Opening the pot to check, which lets the steam out.
steps.fix: Trust the time; the seal shows the pot is closed.

steps.do: Break the seal with a knife and lift the lid away from you. The meat should pull from the bone and reach about 195°F (90°C). Spoon off excess fat, and if the sauce is thin, lift the lamb out and boil the sauce until it coats a spoon.
steps.look: Meat falling away from the bone in a thick, rich sauce.
steps.mistake: Meat still firm.
steps.fix: Reseal with foil and cook 30 minutes more.

steps.do: Sprinkle with rose water, lift the leg to a warm platter and spoon over the sauce. Serve with naan or sheermal, red onion rings, mint, coriander and lime.
steps.look: A glossy, dark, spiced leg and a fragrant sauce.
steps.mistake: Carving it into neat slices; it falls apart.
steps.fix: Pull it apart with two forks at the table.

science: Dum cooking traps steam in a sealed pot, so the lamb cooks in moist heat just below boiling for hours. That converts the leg's collagen into gelatin, making the meat fall from the bone while the steam stops it drying. Raw papaya contains papain, a protein-digesting enzyme that softens the surface of the meat; yoghurt's acid and calcium also loosen surface proteins. Deep scoring lets marinade and salt reach the meat near the bone, where flavour would otherwise never get. Frying the onions caramelises their sugars and creates Maillard flavours, giving the sauce body and sweetness. Rose water goes in only at the end, because its volatile aroma compounds would cook away in the long dum.
plating: Set the leg on a warm oval platter on a bed of thinly sliced red onion, spoon the dark sauce over, and scatter with mint, coriander and a few saffron threads. Arrange lime wedges round it and serve warm naan in a basket beside it.

pairing.drink: A Côte-Rôtie or a ripe Shiraz: smoky, peppery Syrah stands up to warm spices and the rich lamb.
pairing.brennans: René Rostaing ‘Ampodium’ Côte-Rôtie 2012: a mature Syrah from the Brennan's list with smoke and pepper to stand up to the spiced lamb.

variations: Use a whole shoulder of lamb, which is more forgiving.
Cook lamb shanks the same way, about 2 1/2 hours.
Make a dum biryani by layering the cooked lamb with parboiled rice and sealing again for 30 minutes.
safety: Lamb should reach at least 145°F (63°C); for this dish it reaches about 195°F (90°C) to fall apart.
Marinate in the fridge, never at room temperature, and discard leftover marinade.
Breaking the seal releases a rush of steam: lift the lid away from your face.

title: Bebek Betutu (Balinese Spiced Duck)
summary: Balinese bebek betutu: a whole duck rubbed and stuffed with base genep, the island's pounded spice paste, wrapped in banana leaves, steamed, then roasted slowly until it is fragrant and falling apart. It is in the course because it combines pounding a complex paste, steaming and roasting into one long cook that rewards control.
skills: a basa genep paste pounded from many roots
stuffing and coating a whole duck
equipment: Large mortar and pestle or a food processor
Large steamer or a roasting tin with a rack and foil cover
Banana leaves, enough to wrap the duck (or baking parchment)

ingredients.item: Red chillies, long and bird's eye mixed
Fresh turmeric, sliced (or 2 tsp (6 g) ground)
Cassava leaves or kale, blanched and chopped

mise: Pat the duck dry, remove excess fat from the cavity opening, and prick the skin all over without piercing the meat.
Pass banana leaves quickly over a flame or dip in hot water to soften them.

timeline.do: Pound the base genep; fry it; rub and stuff the duck.
Wrap in leaves and foil; steam 1 hour.
Roast at 300°F (150°C) for 2 1/2 to 3 hours.
Unwrap and roast at 400°F (200°C) for 15 minutes to colour.
Rest; make the sambal matah.
Serve with rice and sambal.

steps.do: Pound the base genep: start with salt, chillies, pepper and coriander seeds, then add the hard ingredients (galangal, turmeric, ginger, kencur, lemongrass), then candlenuts, shallots and garlic, and finally the shrimp paste and palm sugar, pounding each to a paste before adding the next, for about 20 minutes.
steps.look: A thick, bright orange-yellow paste with an intense aroma of turmeric and citrus.
steps.mistake: Adding everything at once, which leaves fibrous lumps.
steps.fix: Pound in stages; finish briefly in a small blender if needed.

steps.do: Heat the coconut oil in the wok over medium heat and fry the paste with the lime leaves and salam leaves, stirring, for 8 to 10 minutes until it darkens and the oil separates.
steps.look: A darker, fragrant paste with oil shining round the edges.
steps.mistake: Frying over high heat, which burns the paste.
steps.fix: Keep the heat medium and stir constantly.

steps.do: Cool the paste. Mix one third of it with the cassava leaves and lime juice and stuff the duck cavity. Rub the rest all over and under the skin.
steps.look: A duck evenly coated in orange paste, the cavity filled with green leaves.
steps.mistake: Packing the cavity tightly, so it cooks unevenly.
steps.fix: Fill loosely.

steps.do: Close the cavity with a skewer and tie the legs. Wrap the duck in layers of banana leaf, then in two layers of heavy foil, and tie with string.
steps.look: A neat, tight parcel.
steps.mistake: Loose wrapping, so juices leak out.
steps.fix: Add another layer of foil.

steps.do: Steam the parcel on a rack over 2 inches (5 cm) of boiling water, tightly covered, for 1 hour over medium-high heat.
steps.look: Steam rising and a fragrance coming through the foil.
steps.mistake: Letting the steamer run dry.
steps.fix: Check the water every 20 minutes and top up with boiling water.

steps.do: Transfer the parcel to a roasting tin and roast at 300°F (150°C) for 2 1/2 to 3 hours until the thigh meat is falling from the bone and at least 175°F (79°C).
steps.look: A soft, yielding parcel and rich smell.
steps.mistake: Not cooking it long enough, so the duck is tough.
steps.fix: Return it for another 30 minutes.

steps.do: Unwrap the top of the parcel, pour off the fat and juices into a bowl and skim. Raise the oven to 400°F (200°C) and roast the duck uncovered for 15 minutes until the skin colours.
steps.look: Deep golden skin and a darker paste on top.
steps.mistake: Leaving the fat in the parcel, so the skin stays soggy.
steps.fix: Pour off all the juices first; keep them for spooning over.

steps.do: Rest 10 minutes. Make the sambal matah by mixing sliced shallots, lemongrass, chilli, lime leaves, salt, lime juice and coconut oil.
steps.look: A fresh, raw relish with a sharp, aromatic smell.
steps.mistake: Making the sambal too early, so it goes limp.
steps.fix: Make it just before serving.

steps.do: Pull the duck into pieces or carve, and serve with the stuffing, the skimmed juices, rice and sambal matah.
steps.look: Moist, spiced meat falling from the bone.
steps.mistake: Serving without the cooking juices.
steps.fix: Spoon the skimmed juices over the meat.

science: Base genep is a fat-soluble flavour system: turmeric's curcumin, galangal, ginger and chilli capsaicin all dissolve into oil, which is why the paste is fried until the oil separates. Frying also cooks off the raw harshness of shallot and garlic. Steaming in a sealed parcel heats the duck evenly in moist heat, while slow roasting below the boiling point renders fat and turns collagen to gelatin, so the meat becomes tender. Banana leaves add a subtle grassy aroma and protect the meat from direct heat. A final blast of high heat dries and browns the skin through Maillard reactions.
plating: Serve on a banana leaf on a large platter, the duck pulled into large pieces with the green stuffing piled beside it and the cooking juices spooned over. Set a mound of steamed rice and a bowl of sambal matah alongside, garnished with fried shallots.

pairing.drink: An aromatic Gewurztraminer or an off-dry Riesling: lychee and spice echo turmeric and galangal, and a touch of sweetness tames the chilli.
pairing.brennans: Albert Boxler Pinot Gris 2020: a rich Alsace Pinot Gris from the Brennan's list with the texture and spice to meet the duck and base genep.

variations: Ayam betutu: use a whole chicken, steaming 45 minutes and roasting 1 1/2 hours.
Grill duck legs coated with the paste over charcoal.
Roast the duck in an earthenware pot buried in embers, as in Bali.
safety: Duck legs and thighs must reach at least 165°F (74°C); for tenderness this dish takes them above 175°F (79°C).
Wear gloves when handling turmeric and chillies; turmeric stains.
Open the foil parcel away from your face to avoid hot steam.

title: Palm Nut Soup with Fufu
summary: Ghanaian palm nut soup: goat or chicken simmered with smoked fish in a broth of palm nut cream, tomato, onion and scotch bonnet, skimmed of its red oil and served with stretchy, pounded fufu. It is in the course because it trains skimming a rich soup to clarity, and pounding starch to an elastic dough by hand.
skills: extracting palm fruit cream by hand
a light soup with smoked fish and goat
equipment: Large pot for boiling cassava and plantain
Large mortar and pestle (asanka or wooden mortar) or a food processor
Bowl of cold water for wetting hands

ingredients.item: Goat meat on the bone, in 2 inch (5 cm) pieces (or bone-in chicken thighs)
Palm nut cream (tinned palm nut concentrate)
Smoked mackerel or smoked herring, flaked, bones removed
Garden eggs (African aubergines), or small aubergines
Cassava (yuca), peeled and cut into chunks, woody core removed

mise: Blend half the onion with the ginger and garlic into a paste.
Peel the cassava and plantains; cut into 2 inch (5 cm) chunks and keep them in cold water.

timeline.do: Steam the goat with onion paste and salt for 15 minutes.
Boil the tomatoes and onion, blend, add with palm cream and water.
Simmer 1 1/2 hours, skimming the oil.
Boil the cassava and plantain.
Pound the fufu.
Add smoked fish and garden eggs.
Shape fufu; ladle soup round it.

steps.do: Put the goat in the large pot with the onion paste, sliced onion and 1 tsp (5 g) salt. Cover and steam in its own juices over medium heat for 15 minutes, stirring, until the meat releases liquid and smells fragrant.
steps.look: The meat turning grey and releasing juices, and a strong aroma of onion and ginger.
steps.mistake: Adding water too early, so the meat does not absorb the seasoning.
steps.fix: Let it cook in its own juices first.

steps.do: Add the whole tomatoes, scotch bonnet and 2 cups (480 ml) water, cover and simmer for 10 minutes. Lift out the tomatoes and chilli, blend them smooth, and sieve back into the pot.
steps.look: A smooth red purée with no seeds or skins.
steps.mistake: Blending the scotch bonnet with the seeds if you want mild heat.
steps.fix: Leave the chilli whole and remove it later for less heat.

steps.do: Put the palm nut cream into a bowl with 2 cups (480 ml) hot water and work it with your hand for 2 minutes, squeezing the fibres as you would fresh pounded palm fruit. Pour it through the sieve into the pot, pressing the fibres with your hand until only dry strands remain. Add the remaining water and bring to a simmer.
steps.look: A deep orange-red broth and a small handful of pale, dry fibres left in the sieve.
steps.mistake: Not sieving the palm cream, so fibres stay in the soup.
steps.fix: Sieve it well, squeezing the fibres by hand; they hold a surprising amount of cream.

steps.do: Simmer uncovered for 1 1/2 hours, stirring occasionally. As red oil rises to the surface, skim it off with a ladle into a bowl, leaving a thin film.
steps.look: A layer of bright red oil gathering on the surface, and a broth that thickens and turns glossy.
steps.mistake: Leaving all the oil on, so the soup is greasy and heavy.
steps.fix: Skim regularly; keep some oil for flavour.

steps.do: Meanwhile, boil the cassava and plantain in salted water for 20 to 25 minutes until a knife slides in easily. Drain.
steps.look: Soft, tender chunks that crush under a fork.
steps.mistake: Undercooking them, so the fufu is lumpy.
steps.fix: Boil 5 minutes more.

steps.do: Pound the cassava and plantain while hot in the mortar, a few pieces at a time, folding with a wet hand between strokes, for 10 to 15 minutes until smooth, stretchy and elastic. Or process in a food processor for 3 minutes, then knead with wet hands.
steps.look: A smooth, stretchy, slightly glossy dough that pulls in strands.
steps.mistake: Pounding when it has cooled, which makes it lumpy.
steps.fix: Pound while hot; return to a warm pan with a splash of water if it stiffens.

steps.do: Add the smoked fish and garden eggs to the soup and simmer 10 minutes. Check that the meat is tender and season with salt.
steps.look: Tender goat, flakes of smoked fish, and a rich, smoky, peppery broth.
steps.mistake: Adding the fish too early, so it breaks up and disappears.
steps.fix: Add it only in the last 10 minutes.

steps.do: Wet your hands and shape the fufu into smooth balls the size of a large orange. Set each in a deep bowl and ladle the soup round it, with meat and fish.
steps.look: Smooth, white balls surrounded by a glossy orange soup.
steps.mistake: Shaping with dry hands, so it sticks.
steps.fix: Keep a bowl of cold water to wet your hands.

science: Palm nut cream is an emulsion of red palm oil, water and plant fibre. As the soup simmers, the emulsion breaks and the oil rises because it is less dense than water; skimming it controls richness while leaving some for flavour and colour from carotenoids. The goat's collagen turns to gelatin during the long simmer, giving body. Fufu is stretchy because cooked cassava and plantain starch gelatinise when boiled, and pounding while hot aligns and bonds the swollen starch molecules into an elastic network, much like kneading. If it cools, the starch begins to set and the dough turns lumpy. Smoked fish adds savoury, smoky depth from compounds made during smoking.
plating: Set a smooth ball of fufu in the centre of a deep, wide bowl. Ladle the soup round it so the fufu stands like an island, with pieces of goat, smoked fish and a garden egg arranged in the broth. Serve with a bowl of water for rinsing fingers, as fufu is eaten by hand.

pairing.drink: A cold, crisp lager or a fruity, chilled Beaujolais: the beer refreshes against the scotch bonnet, and the light red handles the smoky, rich broth.
pairing.brennans: Louis Jadot Beaujolais-Villages 2021 (375 ml): a chilled, fruity Beaujolais from the Brennan's list with freshness to cut the rich palm soup.

variations: Use beef, chicken or snails instead of goat.
Serve with omo tuo (rice balls) or banku instead of fufu.
Make abenkwan from fresh palm fruit, boiled and pounded.
safety: Cook goat or chicken to at least 165°F (74°C); after the long simmer it will be far above this.
Cassava must be peeled, cored and boiled thoroughly; never eat it raw.
Wear gloves for scotch bonnets; wash hands thoroughly afterwards.
Pounding hot starch: keep fingers clear of the pestle and wet your hands only with cold water.
