title: Torta Rogel
summary: Argentina's torta rogel: eight wafer-thin, crisp pastry discs rich with egg yolk, stacked with thick dulce de leche and crowned with a mountain of Italian meringue scorched at the tips. It is in the course because rolling eight identical paper-thin discs and cooking a sugar syrup to the exact stage for the meringue are both tests of precision.
skills: rolling and baking many paper thin layers
equipment: Rolling pin and a large sheet of parchment
6 inch (15 cm) plate or cake ring as a template
Two baking trays lined with parchment

ingredients.item: Dulce de leche repostero (thick pastry dulce de leche)
ingredients.note: the thick kind that holds its shape

ingredients.item: Cream of tartar or lemon juice

mise: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C).
Bring the dulce de leche to room temperature so it spreads easily.
Cut eight squares of parchment slightly larger than the template.

timeline.do: Make the dough; rest 30 minutes.
Roll and bake eight discs, 5 to 7 minutes each batch; cool.
Stack with dulce de leche.
Make the Italian meringue; pile on; torch.
Rest at least 3 hours so the discs soften slightly.
Slice with a hot serrated knife.

steps.do: Mix the flour and salt in a bowl, add the yolks, butter, milk and brandy and work together with your fingertips, then knead for 3 to 4 minutes on a clean surface until the dough is smooth, firm and no longer sticky.
steps.look: A smooth, firm, pale yellow dough that springs back slowly.
steps.mistake: A dough too dry to come together.
steps.fix: Add milk a teaspoon at a time.

steps.do: Wrap the dough and rest it at room temperature for 30 minutes so the gluten relaxes and it rolls thin without shrinking.
steps.look: A dough that no longer pulls back when pressed.
steps.mistake: Rolling straight away, so the discs shrink in the oven.
steps.fix: Rest it longer.

steps.do: Divide the dough into 8 equal pieces, about 1 1/4 oz (34 g) each. Roll each on parchment into a circle a little larger than 6 inches (15 cm) and about 1/16 inch (1.5 mm) thick, the thickness of two coins stacked. Cut round the template.
steps.look: Eight discs so thin you can almost see the paper through them.
steps.mistake: Rolling unevenly, so thin areas burn.
steps.fix: Roll from the centre outwards and turn the paper often.

steps.do: Prick each disc all over with a fork, slide them on their paper onto the trays and bake for 5 to 7 minutes until pale golden and dry. They crisp as they cool.
steps.look: Pale gold, flat, dry discs.
steps.mistake: Baking too long, so they turn brown and bitter.
steps.fix: Watch them from 4 minutes; take each out as it colours.

steps.do: Cool the discs flat on a rack. Set the flattest one aside for the top.
steps.look: Crisp, flat discs that snap.
steps.mistake: Stacking them warm, so they steam soft.
steps.fix: Cool completely.

steps.do: Set one disc on the cake board, spread about 1/3 cup (55 g) dulce de leche evenly to the edge, and continue with the rest, pressing gently each time, finishing with the flattest disc.
steps.look: An even tower with a thin line of caramel between every layer.
steps.mistake: Pressing too hard, which cracks the discs.
steps.fix: Press gently with your palm; a cracked disc can go in the middle.

steps.do: Make the Italian meringue: put the sugar and water in the saucepan and boil without stirring until it reaches 244°F (118°C). When the syrup reaches 230°F (110°C), start whisking the egg whites with the cream of tartar to soft peaks.
steps.look: Clear syrup bubbling thickly; whites at soft peaks just as the syrup hits 244°F (118°C).
steps.mistake: Stirring the syrup, which makes it crystallise.
steps.fix: Brush the pan sides with a wet brush; never stir.

steps.do: With the mixer running, pour the hot syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl into the whites, avoiding the whisk. Beat on high for 6 to 8 minutes until the meringue is glossy, stiff and the bowl is just warm.
steps.look: A glossy, thick meringue holding stiff peaks.
steps.mistake: Pouring syrup onto the whisk, so it spins into sugar threads.
steps.fix: Pour down the side.

steps.do: Pile the meringue on top of the cake and pull it into peaks with the back of a spoon. Scorch the peaks with the blowtorch until golden and dark at the tips.
steps.look: Golden, toasted peaks on white meringue.
steps.mistake: Torching too close, so the meringue burns.
steps.fix: Hold the flame 3 inches (8 cm) away and keep moving.

steps.do: Rest the cake at room temperature for at least 3 hours, then slice with a hot serrated knife.
steps.look: Discs softened slightly so the cake cuts cleanly.
steps.mistake: Cutting at once, so the crisp discs shatter.
steps.fix: Wait; the discs absorb moisture from the dulce de leche and soften.

science: The discs are made with egg yolk and little butter, so they bake into a crisp, short pastry. Thin rolling and pricking stop them puffing. Repostero dulce de leche is cooked longer and holds less water than spreading dulce de leche, so it does not soak the discs through. Italian meringue is made by pouring sugar syrup at 244°F (118°C) into whipped whites: the heat partly sets the proteins and the dissolved sugar stabilises the foam, giving a glossy meringue that holds its shape for hours.
plating: Set a tall slice on its side on a plate to show the eight layers of crisp pastry and caramel under the toasted meringue. Serve alone, with a cup of coffee.

pairing.drink: A cup of strong espresso, or a tawny port: bitterness or nutty sweetness balance the dulce de leche.
pairing.brennans: Niepoort Colheita Port 1997 (375 ml): an aged tawny-style port from the Brennan's list with caramel and nut flavours that match the dulce de leche.

variations: Use a Swiss meringue instead of Italian meringue.
Add a layer of chopped walnuts.
Make mini rogels as individual stacks.
safety: Syrup at 244°F (118°C) does not fully pasteurise the whites, so use pasteurised egg whites.
Hot sugar syrup causes serious burns: pour carefully and keep children away.
Blowtorch: keep the flame away from your hand and use a heat-proof board.

title: Sans Rival
summary: The Filipino sans rival: crisp, chewy layers of cashew meringue (dacquoise) sandwiched with rich French buttercream and covered with toasted chopped cashews. It is in the course because it pairs a nut meringue baked slowly to crispness with a buttercream built on cooked sugar syrup, two classic pastry techniques.
skills: cashew dacquoise layers piped and baked
a French buttercream made with hot syrup and yolks
equipment: Two baking trays lined with parchment
Small heavy saucepan and sugar thermometer

ingredients.note: 1 cup (120 g) for meringue, 1/2 cup (60 g) for coating

mise: Heat the oven to 275°F (135°C).

Toast the cashews at 325°F (160°C) for 8 to 10 minutes until golden; cool. Grind 1 cup (120 g) finely with 2 tbsp (25 g) of the meringue sugar; chop the rest coarsely.

timeline.do: Toast and grind cashews; make the meringue.
Bake meringue layers 35 to 45 minutes; cool.
Make the French buttercream.
Layer, coat and cover with cashews; chill 2 hours.
Slice with a hot knife.

steps.do: Whip the egg whites with the cream of tartar to soft peaks, then add the remaining meringue sugar a spoonful at a time and whip to stiff, glossy peaks, about 5 minutes.
steps.look: Glossy, stiff peaks that do not move when the bowl is tipped.
steps.mistake: Adding sugar too fast, so the meringue weeps.
steps.fix: Add slowly and beat until smooth.

steps.do: Fold the ground cashews into the meringue gently with a large spatula in two additions, cutting down through the middle and turning the bowl a quarter turn with each stroke, about 15 strokes in all.
steps.look: A thick, speckled meringue that still holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Overfolding, so the meringue deflates and runs.
steps.fix: Fold just until no streaks remain.

steps.do: Spread the meringue evenly within the three rectangles, about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick. Bake at 275°F (135°C) for 35 to 45 minutes until golden and crisp on the outside.
steps.look: Pale gold layers that lift from the paper.
steps.mistake: Taking them out too early, so they are soft and stick.
steps.fix: Bake 10 minutes more; they crisp as they cool.

steps.do: Cool the layers on the paper, then peel off carefully and trim to neat rectangles with a serrated knife.
steps.look: Neat, crisp rectangles.
steps.mistake: Peeling warm meringue, which breaks.
steps.fix: Wait until cold.

steps.do: Make the buttercream: whip the yolks in the mixer until pale. Boil the sugar and water to 240°F (116°C), then pour it in a thin stream into the whipping yolks. Whip until the bowl is cool to the touch, about 8 minutes.
steps.look: A pale, thick, mousse-like yolk mixture.
steps.mistake: Adding butter while the mixture is warm, so it melts.
steps.fix: Whip until the bowl feels cool.

steps.do: Add the butter a tablespoon at a time, whipping well after each, then the vanilla and salt. Whip until smooth and fluffy.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy buttercream.
steps.mistake: Curdled buttercream from cold butter.
steps.fix: Keep whipping; warm the bowl briefly if it stays curdled.

steps.do: Place a meringue layer on the board and spread a layer of buttercream 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick. Repeat with the second layer, then top with the third. Cover the top and sides with buttercream.
steps.look: A neat, straight-sided block.
steps.mistake: Pressing too hard, so the meringue cracks.
steps.fix: Spread lightly with the palette knife.

steps.do: Press the 1/2 cup (60 g) chopped cashews onto the sides and top with a cupped palm, catching the falls on the board, then chill the cake for 2 hours until the buttercream is firm.
steps.look: A cake completely covered in golden cashews.
steps.mistake: Leaving it at room temperature, so the buttercream softens.
steps.fix: Chill to set.

steps.do: Cut the chilled cake into slices 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between every cut, pressing straight down in one stroke.
steps.look: Clean slices with crisp layers and smooth buttercream.
steps.mistake: Using a cold knife.
steps.fix: Dip in hot water and wipe between cuts.

science: A dacquoise is a meringue with ground nuts folded in. The nuts add fat, which weakens the foam slightly, so the meringue must be whipped stiff and folded gently. French buttercream is built on egg yolks cooked by a hot sugar syrup at 240°F (116°C): the syrup heats the yolks and the sugar stabilises the foam. plating: Set a slice on a plate on its side, so the crisp meringue layers and pale buttercream show. Add a few whole toasted cashews on the side.

pairing.brennans: Château Climens Barsac Premier Cru Classé 2010: a Barsac from the Brennan's list whose honeyed sweetness and acidity cut through buttercream.

Make silvanas, small meringue and buttercream biscuits coated in crumbs.
Flavour the buttercream with coffee or mango.
safety: The yolks are cooked by syrup at 240°F (116°C), but do not reach full pasteurisation; use pasteurised eggs for anyone vulnerable.
Hot sugar syrup: pour carefully and keep hands away from the whisk.
Keep the cake refrigerated.

title: Medovik

equipment: Heatproof bowl and pan for a water bath
6 inch (15 cm) plate or cake ring as a template
Food processor or rolling pin for crumbs

Cut seven sheets of parchment slightly larger than the template.

Take the cake out of the fridge.
Slice and serve.

steps.do: Melt the honey, butter and sugar in the bowl over simmering water, stirring, until the sugar dissolves. Whisk in the bicarbonate of soda; it will foam up and turn a deep amber colour in about 1 to 2 minutes.

steps.mistake: Taking it off too early, so the flavour is weak, or too late, so it tastes burnt.
steps.fix: Stop when it is a rich amber, like dark honey.

steps.do: Off the heat, whisk in the egg quickly so it does not scramble, then stir in the flour and salt to form a soft, warm dough.
steps.look: A smooth, soft, golden dough.
steps.mistake: Adding the egg to very hot honey, which scrambles it.
steps.fix: Cool the honey for 1 minute first and whisk fast.

steps.do: Divide the dough into 7 equal pieces while warm. Roll each on a floured parchment sheet into a circle about 1/16 inch (2 mm) thick, slightly larger than 6 inches (15 cm).
steps.look: Thin, even circles of dough.
steps.mistake: Rolling cold dough, which cracks.
steps.fix: Keep the dough warm by covering it.

steps.do: Prick each circle all over with a fork, slide it on its paper onto a tray and bake at 350°F (180°C) for 4 to 5 minutes until golden brown.
steps.look: Golden brown, crisp layers smelling of honey.
steps.mistake: Overbaking, so the layers turn bitter.
steps.fix: Watch closely from 3 minutes.

steps.do: While still hot, trim each layer round the template with a sharp knife. Keep the trimmings.
steps.look: Neat circles and a pile of crisp scraps.
steps.mistake: Trimming cold layers, which crack.
steps.fix: Trim immediately.

steps.do: Grind the cooled trimmings in the food processor for 30 seconds, or crush them under a rolling pin in a bag, into fine, even crumbs about 1/2 cup (50 g) in all.
steps.look: Golden, fine crumbs.
steps.mistake: Leaving large pieces.
steps.fix: Grind finer.

steps.do: Make the cream: whip the double cream to soft peaks, then fold in the sour cream, condensed milk and vanilla until smooth.
steps.look: A smooth, thick, tangy cream.
steps.mistake: Overwhipping, so the cream splits.
steps.fix: Stop at soft peaks.

steps.do: Place a layer on the board and spread 1/3 cup (70 g) cream over it. Repeat with all layers, then cover the top and sides with the remaining cream.
steps.look: A neat, even stack with cream between each layer.
steps.mistake: Using too little cream, so the cake stays dry.
steps.fix: Be generous; the cream softens the layers.

steps.do: Press the crumbs over the top and sides of the cake with a cupped palm, in an even layer about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick, until no cream shows.
steps.look: A cake completely covered in golden crumbs.
steps.mistake: Leaving gaps.
steps.fix: Use more crumbs.

steps.do: Cover the cake loosely with an upturned bowl or cling film and chill for at least 12 hours, ideally 24, then let it stand 30 minutes before slicing into 4 wedges.
steps.look: A soft, tender cake that cuts cleanly.
steps.mistake: Serving on the same day, when the layers are still crisp.

plating: Set a tall slice on its side on a plate to show the thin golden layers and white cream. Add a small drizzle of honey on the plate and a few fresh berries.

pairing.drink: A black tea with lemon, or a sweet Tokaji: tea refreshes, and the wine's honeyed notes echo the cake.

variations: Use dulce de leche in the cream.
Add a layer of chopped walnuts.
Make a chocolate medovik with cocoa in the dough.
safety: The honey mixture is very hot: handle the bowl with gloves.
Keep the cake refrigerated and eat within 4 days.

title: Lapis Legit
summary: Indonesian lapis legit: a rich butter cake of egg yolks and warm spices, built one thin layer at a time under the oven's top grill (broiler) element until it holds fifteen or more stripes. baking eighteen thin layers one at a time under the grill
equipment: 6 inch (15 cm) square cake tin, lined with parchment
Stand mixer with paddle and whisk
Flat-bottomed tamper or a small glass to press layers
Oven with a top grill element

ingredients.item: Lapis spice (spekkoek mix, or mix cinnamon, cardamom, clove, nutmeg)

mise: Have everything at room temperature.
Heat the oven grill (top element) to high, and the oven itself to 350°F (180°C) for the first layer.
Sift the flour with the spice.

timeline.do: Cream butter and condensed milk; whip yolks and whites.
Fold the batter.
Bake the first layer; then grill each layer 4 to 6 minutes, about 15 layers.
Bake the finished cake 10 minutes.
Cool completely.
Slice.

steps.do: Cream the soft butter and condensed milk in the mixer with the paddle on medium-high for 5 to 7 minutes, scraping the bowl twice, until pale, fluffy and almost white.
steps.look: A light, whipped butter that has increased noticeably in volume.
steps.mistake: Starting with cold butter, so the mixture stays dense and the cake is heavy.
steps.fix: Let the butter soften to about 65°F (18°C), where it dents easily but is not greasy.

steps.do: In a second bowl, whisk the 8 yolks, 2 whites, sugar, vanilla and salt on high for 6 to 8 minutes until very pale, thick and doubled in volume.
steps.look: A thick, pale yellow foam that falls in a ribbon.
steps.mistake: Stopping as soon as it looks frothy, so the cake has no lift.
steps.fix: Keep whisking until a ribbon holds on the surface for 2 seconds.

steps.do: Fold the creamed butter into the egg foam in three additions with a large spatula, then sift the flour and spice over and fold gently until no streaks remain. Weigh the batter so you can divide it into equal layers, about 1 1/4 oz (35 g) each.
steps.look: A smooth, thick, spiced batter, about 1 1/4 lb (570 g) in all.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard, which deflates the foam and gives a dense, greasy cake.
steps.fix: Fold with broad, gentle strokes; a few streaks of butter are better than overmixing.

steps.do: Spread 4 tbsp (60 g) batter evenly over the base of the lined 6 inch (15 cm) tin with the small offset palette knife and bake on the middle shelf at 350°F (180°C) for 8 to 10 minutes until set and golden.
steps.look: A firm, golden first layer that does not wobble.
steps.mistake: Making the first layer thick, so it never cooks through underneath the rest.
steps.fix: Keep it thin; bake 2 minutes more if the centre still looks wet.

steps.do: Switch the oven to the top grill element on high and move a shelf so the top of the tin sits 5 to 6 inches (13 to 15 cm) below the element. Brush the cake lightly with melted butter, spread about 2 1/2 tbsp (35 g) batter evenly over it, and grill for 4 to 6 minutes until evenly golden brown.
steps.look: An evenly browned layer with a slightly darker edge, the batter set right across.
steps.mistake: Placing the tin too close to the element, so the top burns before the layer sets.
steps.fix: Lower the shelf; if one side browns faster, turn the tin halfway through.

steps.do: Take out the tin, press the new layer gently all over with the flat tamper to drive out air, and prick any bubbles with a skewer before the next layer goes on.
steps.look: A flat, even surface with no bubbles or domes.
steps.mistake: Skipping the press, so air pockets build up and the stripes become wavy.
steps.fix: Press every layer; a bubble that has set can be pricked and pressed flat.

steps.do: Repeat the brush, spread, grill and press sequence until all the batter is used, about 15 layers in all, setting a timer for every layer and keeping each one the same weight.
steps.look: A tall cake with even, sharp, dark and light stripes.
steps.mistake: Losing track of time between layers, so one burns black and turns bitter.
steps.fix: Set a timer every time; scrape off a burnt layer with a knife before adding the next.

steps.do: Switch the oven back to bake at 350°F (180°C), lower the shelf to the middle and bake the cake for 10 minutes to cook through. A skewer pushed into the centre should come out clean.
steps.look: A firm, springy, golden top and a clean skewer.
steps.mistake: Leaving the centre undercooked, which collapses as it cools.

steps.do: Cool completely in the tin, about 2 hours, then turn out and cut into slices 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick with a long, sharp knife, wiping the blade between cuts.
steps.look: Neat slices showing fifteen or more fine, even stripes.
steps.mistake: Cutting the cake warm, so the soft butter layers smear and squash.
steps.fix: Let it cool fully; chill 20 minutes for the cleanest slices.

science: Lapis legit is a butter cake with very little flour and many egg yolks, so its structure comes from egg proteins and emulsified butter. Creaming the butter traps air, and whipping the eggs adds more. Each layer is cooked under intense radiant heat from the top grill element, which sets and browns only the surface, creating the dark stripes through Maillard reactions and caramelisation. Pressing each layer removes air bubbles and keeps the layers even. The final bake cooks the whole cake through. The high fat content keeps the cake moist for days.
plating: Cut thin slices and lay them on a plate in a fan so the many stripes show. Serve with tea or coffee, as in Indonesia.

pairing.drink: A spiced chai, or a late harvest Gewurztraminer: the spices in the cake meet the wine's aromatic sweetness.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives 2007: a late harvest Alsace wine from the Brennan's list with spice to echo the lapis spices.

variations: Lapis legit prunes: lay prunes on some layers.
Make a pandan version with alternating green layers.
Add a layer of cheese, as in Indonesian lapis keju.
safety: The grill element is extremely hot: use oven gloves every time you take the tin out.
Keep the oven door open only as long as needed.

title: Dobos Torta
summary: Hungary's Dobos torta: six thin sponge layers stacked with chocolate buttercream and topped with a hard caramel lid cut into wedges, propped on rosettes of cream. It is in the course because it combines thin sponges, a buttercream built on cooked syrup, and the unforgiving timing of cutting caramel before it sets hard.
skills: a caramel top cut into wedges before it sets
equipment: Two baking trays lined with parchment
mise: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).
Draw six 6 inch (15 cm) circles on parchment and turn them over.
Oil a sheet of parchment and a knife for the caramel.

timeline.do: Make the sponge; bake six layers 6 to 8 minutes each batch; cool flat.
Make the chocolate buttercream.
Make the caramel top and cut into wedges.
Layer, coat, press on walnuts, set the wedges; chill 2 hours.
Slice along the wedges.

steps.do: Whip the 3 egg whites to soft peaks, about 2 minutes, then add half the sponge sugar and whip to firm, glossy peaks. In a second bowl, beat the yolks with the remaining sugar for 3 to 4 minutes until pale and ribboning. Fold the yolks into the whites, then sift the flour over and fold it in with the cooled melted butter.
steps.look: A light, pale, airy batter with no streaks of flour.
steps.mistake: Stirring rather than folding, so the batter deflates and the thin layers bake flat and tough.
steps.fix: Fold with broad, gentle strokes, turning the bowl; the batter should still hold soft mounds.

steps.do: Divide the batter among the six drawn circles, about 3 1/2 tbsp (55 g) each, and spread it thinly and evenly to the lines with the offset palette knife. Bake one tray at a time at 400°F (200°C) for 6 to 8 minutes until golden at the edges.
steps.look: Thin, pale gold discs, slightly darker at the edges, springy to the touch.
steps.mistake: Overbaking, so the layers turn brittle and crack when stacked.
steps.fix: Check from 5 minutes; they are done the moment the edges colour.

steps.do: Peel the layers off the paper while still warm, within 2 minutes of leaving the oven, and cool them flat under a sheet of parchment and a light board.
steps.look: Flat, even layers that bend without breaking.
steps.mistake: Leaving them on the paper to cool, where they stick and tear.
steps.fix: Brush the back of the paper with a damp cloth to release a stuck layer.

steps.do: Make the chocolate buttercream: boil the 1/2 cup (100 g) sugar and 2 tbsp (30 ml) water to 240°F (116°C). Pour it in a thin stream into the yolks while whipping on high, and whip for 6 to 8 minutes until the bowl is cool. Beat in the soft butter a tablespoon at a time, then the cooled melted chocolate.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, dark chocolate buttercream that holds soft peaks.
steps.mistake: Adding the butter while the yolks are warm, so it melts into a thin soup.
steps.fix: Chill the bowl for 10 minutes and whip again; it will come back.

steps.do: Set the best sponge layer on the oiled parchment. Cook the 1/2 cup (100 g) caramel sugar with the lemon juice in a clean heavy pan over medium heat, swirling but not stirring, until it melts and turns a clear mid amber, 340°F (170°C). Pour it straight over the layer and spread quickly with an oiled palette knife.
steps.look: A thin, glossy, amber sheet of caramel covering the sponge evenly.
steps.mistake: Letting the caramel go dark mahogany, which tastes acrid.
steps.fix: Take it off at mid amber; it keeps darkening in the pan, so pour without delay.

steps.do: As soon as the caramel stops running, within about 30 seconds, mark it into 8 wedges with the oiled knife, then cut right through each line with firm downward presses.
steps.look: Eight clean wedges of caramel-topped sponge with sharp edges.
steps.mistake: Waiting until it hardens, so the caramel shatters into shards instead of cutting.
steps.fix: Work fast; if it sets, warm the knife in hot water, dry it and press through.

steps.do: Stack the remaining five layers on the board with about 3 tbsp (45 g) buttercream spread between each, then cover the top and sides with a thin, even coat.
steps.look: A neat, level cake with straight sides.
steps.mistake: Uneven filling, so the cake leans.
steps.fix: Weigh or measure the buttercream for each layer.

steps.do: Press the ground walnuts onto the sides with a cupped palm. Pipe 8 rosettes of buttercream round the top edge and prop a caramel wedge on each at the same angle, like the blades of a fan. Chill for 2 hours.
steps.look: A cake crowned with an even fan of shining caramel wedges.
steps.mistake: Laying the wedges flat, which makes them hard to cut and loses the classic look.
steps.fix: Prop each wedge on its rosette at about 30 degrees, all leaning the same way.

steps.do: Slice the chilled cake into 4 portions along the lines of the wedges with a knife dipped in hot water and wiped, two wedges to each portion.
steps.look: Neat slices showing six thin sponge layers and dark buttercream, each with its own caramel crown.
steps.mistake: Cutting through the caramel wedges, which shatters them.
steps.fix: Cut between the wedges, following their lines.

science: Thin sponge layers bake quickly and stay moist because the batter is spread thin. The chocolate buttercream is a French buttercream: yolks heated by sugar syrup at 240°F (116°C) form a stable foam, and butter whisked in makes a smooth emulsion. The caramel lid is sugar melted and browned to about 340°F (170°C); once it cools below about 210°F (100°C), it becomes glass, so it must be cut while still pliable. Lemon juice inverts some of the sucrose into glucose and fructose, preventing crystallisation and keeping the caramel clear.
plating: Set a slice on a plate with the caramel wedge on top, the six thin layers and dark buttercream visible from the side. Serve with a small spoon of whipped cream.

pairing.drink: A Hungarian Tokaji Aszú or a tawny port: honey and nut flavours match the caramel and chocolate.
pairing.brennans: Taylor Fladgate Vintage Port 1977: an aged port from the Brennan's list with dried fruit and nut flavours for chocolate and caramel.

variations: Use a coffee buttercream.
Make a rectangular version for easier slicing.
Leave off the caramel for a simpler chocolate layer cake.
safety: Caramel at 340°F (170°C) causes severe burns: use a long knife and never touch it.
Yolks heated by syrup are not fully pasteurised; use pasteurised eggs for anyone vulnerable.

title: M'hencha (Moroccan Almond Snake)
summary: Moroccan m'hencha, the almond snake: long ropes of almond paste scented with orange blossom and cinnamon, wrapped in buttered phyllo, coiled into a spiral, baked golden and glazed with warm honey. It is in the course because it is a test of handling paper-thin pastry without tearing or letting it dry, and of making a paste that holds its shape in the oven.
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) round cake tin or ovenproof frying pan, buttered

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, soft, for the paste
Egg yolk, beaten with 1 tsp (5 ml) water
Icing sugar and cinnamon, for dusting

mise: Thaw the phyllo in the fridge overnight, still wrapped, then 1 hour at room temperature.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C) and butter the tin.
Lay out a damp towel to keep the phyllo covered at all times.

timeline.do: Make the almond paste; chill 20 minutes.
Roll paste into ropes; wrap in phyllo; coil into the tin.
Glaze and bake 30 to 35 minutes.
Brush with warm honey; scatter almonds.
Cool slightly; dust and slice.

steps.do: Make the paste: blitz the ground almonds, icing sugar, soft butter, egg white, orange blossom water, cinnamon and almond extract in the food processor for 30 to 45 seconds until it forms a smooth, firm paste that holds together when pressed. Chill 20 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, pliable, slightly sticky paste that smells strongly of orange blossom.
steps.mistake: A paste too wet to roll, which spreads and leaks in the oven.
steps.fix: Add ground almonds 1 tbsp (7 g) at a time until it holds its shape.

steps.do: Divide the paste into 3 equal pieces and roll each with lightly sugared hands into a rope about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick and 14 inches (35 cm) long.
steps.look: Three smooth, even ropes.
steps.mistake: Rolling uneven ropes, so the snake bulges.
steps.fix: Roll on the board with flat hands, working from the centre outwards.

steps.do: Lay one sheet of phyllo on the board with a long side towards you, keeping the rest covered. Brush it lightly with melted butter, lay a second sheet on top and brush again.
steps.look: Two thin, buttered sheets with no dry patches.
steps.mistake: Leaving the phyllo uncovered, so it dries and cracks within 2 minutes.
steps.fix: Keep the stack under the damp towel; work quickly.

steps.do: Lay a rope of paste along the long edge, 1 inch (2.5 cm) in from the edge. Roll up the phyllo round the paste firmly but not too tightly, to form a long, thin cylinder.
steps.look: A neat cylinder with the paste in the centre.
steps.mistake: Rolling too tightly, so the phyllo splits when coiled.
steps.fix: Roll snugly but leave a little give.

steps.do: Starting from the centre of the tin, coil the first cylinder into a spiral, seam side down, pushing it gently together like an accordion so it can bend without tearing.
steps.look: A tight spiral at the centre, with small pleats in the pastry.
steps.mistake: Bending the cylinder sharply, which cracks the phyllo.
steps.fix: Push the cylinder together to make soft folds before coiling.

steps.do: Make the other two cylinders the same way and continue the coil, joining each to the end of the last, until the spiral fills the tin.
steps.look: A single snake coiled to the edge of the tin.
steps.mistake: Leaving gaps between the coils.
steps.fix: Push the coils together; they will expand slightly in the oven.

steps.do: Brush the whole surface with the remaining melted butter, then with the egg yolk glaze.
steps.look: A glossy surface with no dry phyllo showing.
steps.mistake: Missing patches, which bake pale and brittle.
steps.fix: Brush every exposed fold.

steps.do: Bake at 350°F (180°C) for 30 to 35 minutes until deep golden brown and crisp.
steps.look: Deep golden, crisp, puffed pastry and a smell of toasted almond.
steps.mistake: Pale, soft phyllo from underbaking.
steps.fix: Bake 5 to 10 minutes more.

steps.do: Warm the honey with 1 tbsp (15 ml) orange blossom water for 1 minute until runny, and brush it over the hot pastry. Scatter with toasted almonds.
steps.look: A glossy, honey-glazed spiral.
steps.mistake: Using cold, thick honey, which tears the pastry.
steps.fix: Always warm it until it pours.

steps.do: Cool for 20 minutes in the tin, then turn out onto a plate. Dust with icing sugar and cinnamon in thin lines and cut into wedges with a serrated knife.
steps.look: A coiled snake with crisp layers and a moist almond centre.
steps.mistake: Cutting it hot, so the paste oozes.
steps.fix: Let it cool and set first.

science: Phyllo is a dough stretched so thin that it is almost all surface. Butter brushed between the sheets separates them, and in the oven the water in the butter and dough turns to steam, puffing the layers, while the fat fries them crisp. Phyllo dries out quickly because it is so thin, which is why it must be kept covered. The almond paste holds its shape because egg white proteins set when heated, binding the ground almonds and sugar. Honey brushed onto hot pastry soaks in slightly while the surface stays crisp. Orange blossom water's aroma comes from compounds such as linalool, which fade with long heating, so a little more goes into the glaze.
plating: Set the whole snake on a round plate and dust it with icing sugar and cinnamon in alternating lines across the spiral. Cut wedges at the table and serve with mint tea.

pairing.drink: Moroccan mint tea, or a sweet Muscat: fresh mint and sweetness match the almond, cinnamon and orange blossom.
pairing.brennans: Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva NV: a sweet fortified wine from the Brennan's list whose nutty sweetness suits almond pastry.

variations: Add chopped dates or pistachios to the almond paste.
Make individual coils as small snails.
Use walnuts instead of almonds.
safety: The tin and honey are very hot when glazing; use oven gloves.
The paste contains raw egg white, which bakes fully at 350°F (180°C) for 30 minutes.

title: Cassata Siciliana
summary: Sicilian cassata: a dome of sponge soaked in maraschino, filled with sweetened sheep's milk ricotta, chocolate and candied fruit, walled in green marzipan, glazed white and decorated with candied fruit. It is in the course because it brings together a smooth ricotta cream, cold marzipan work and a poured glaze, and every element must be chilled to hold its shape.
equipment: 6 inch (15 cm) sloped cake tin or a bowl of the same width
Rolling pin and icing sugar for dusting
Saucepan and thermometer for the glaze

ingredients.item: Sheep's or whole cow's milk ricotta
Candied pumpkin (zuccata) or candied orange, diced
Sponge (pan di Spagna), in sheets 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick

mise: Drain the ricotta in muslin in the fridge for 12 hours.
Chill the marzipan for 30 minutes before rolling.
Line the tin with cling film, leaving an overhang.

timeline.do: Drain the ricotta overnight.
Sieve and sweeten the ricotta; rest 1 hour; fold in chocolate and fruit.
Line the tin with marzipan and sponge; fill; chill 6 hours.
Turn out; glaze; decorate; chill 30 minutes.
Slice the chilled cake into 4 portions with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between every cut.

steps.do: Push the drained ricotta through the fine sieve twice with a spatula, about 5 minutes each pass, until completely smooth; you should have about 14 oz (400 g).
steps.look: A smooth, silky ricotta with no grain.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve, so the cream is grainy.
steps.fix: Sieve twice; it makes the difference.

steps.do: Beat in the sugar and leave for 1 hour so it dissolves fully, then rub a little between your fingers; if gritty, wait 30 minutes more.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy cream with no grit.
steps.mistake: Using it at once, so undissolved sugar makes the cassata weep.
steps.fix: Give it time.

steps.do: Fold the 1 1/2 oz (40 g) chopped chocolate and the candied pumpkin into the sweetened ricotta with a spatula in about 10 strokes, keeping the cream stiff enough to hold a soft peak.
steps.look: A thick cream speckled with chocolate and fruit.
steps.mistake: Overmixing, so the cream loosens.
steps.fix: Fold gently.

steps.do: Roll the cold marzipan between sheets of parchment into a strip 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick and as tall as the tin's sides. Line the sides of the tin, pressing it firmly against the film.
steps.look: A smooth green wall round the tin.
steps.mistake: Rolling warm marzipan, which sweats oil and sticks.
steps.fix: Chill it again and roll between paper.

steps.do: Cut the sponge to fit the base snugly, about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick, and brush it with half the maraschino diluted with the 2 tbsp (30 ml) water.
steps.look: Moist sponge fitted snugly.
steps.mistake: Soaking too much, so the base collapses.
steps.fix: Brush lightly.

steps.do: Spoon in the ricotta cream, level it, and cover with more sponge brushed with liqueur. Fold over the film and chill for at least 6 hours.
steps.look: A firm, set cassata.
steps.mistake: Turning out too early, so it collapses.
steps.fix: Chill longer.

steps.do: Lift the overhanging film, set a flat plate over the tin, turn the cassata out in one movement, and peel off the film slowly, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) at a time.
steps.look: A green-walled dome with a sponge top.
steps.mistake: Tearing the marzipan.
steps.fix: Peel the film slowly.

steps.do: Warm the icing sugar and water to 104°F (40°C), stirring, until it pours like thick cream. Pour over the top in one smooth pass, letting it run down slightly.
steps.look: A glossy, white glaze.
steps.mistake: Overheating, so the glaze sets dull and cracked.
steps.fix: Keep it to 104°F (40°C).

steps.do: Decorate quickly with candied fruit before the glaze sets. Chill 30 minutes, then slice with a hot knife.
steps.look: A colourful, glossy cassata.
steps.mistake: Waiting until the glaze sets, so the fruit will not stick.
steps.fix: Work fast.

science: Ricotta is a soft curd that holds a lot of whey. Draining removes water, and sieving breaks up the curds into a smooth cream. Sugar must dissolve completely: undissolved crystals draw whey out by osmosis, and the cassata weeps inside its marzipan wall. Marzipan is ground almonds and sugar bound with syrup; warm, the almond oil sweats out, so it must be worked cold. The glaze is a simple fondant of icing sugar and water warmed to 104°F (40°C), so it flows smoothly and sets glossy; hotter, the sugar recrystallises and turns dull.
plating: Set the whole cassata on a cake stand so the green marzipan wall, the white glaze and the jewelled candied fruit show. Cut wedges with a hot knife and lay each on its side so the ricotta, chocolate and sponge show.

pairing.drink: A Sicilian Passito di Pantelleria or a Marsala: honeyed apricot and nut notes match the ricotta and candied fruit.
pairing.brennans: Château d’Yquem Sauternes 2016 (375 ml): a great Sauternes from the Brennan's list with the honeyed richness for ricotta and candied fruit.

variations: Make cassatelle, small fried pastries filled with the same ricotta cream.
Use cow's milk ricotta if sheep's is unavailable.
Make a baked cassata in a shortcrust case.
safety: Use pasteurised ricotta and keep the cassata refrigerated, below 40°F (4°C); eat within 2 days.
Maraschino contains alcohol; leave it out for children or substitute orange juice.

title: Turrón de Alicante
summary: Spain's turrón de Alicante: toasted Marcona almonds set in a hard nougat of honey, sugar and egg white, cooked slowly until it snaps, pressed into a frame between wafers and cut into bars. It is in the course because it is cooked by reading the sugar: honey and syrup taken to exact stages, then a long stir to drive out water.
skills: cooking honey and sugar to the hard crack stage
equipment: Saucepans: one small, one medium heavy-based
Stand mixer or hand mixer with a deep bowl
Heatproof bowl and pan for a bain-marie
6 by 4 inch (15 by 10 cm) frame or a small loaf tin lined with parchment
Bowl of cold water for testing
mise: Line the frame with parchment and lay a sheet of wafer paper on the base.
Have the bain-marie set up with water at a bare simmer.
Toast the almonds at 320°F (160°C) for 12 to 15 minutes until pale gold right through; keep warm.

timeline.do: Toast almonds; cook honey and syrup; whip and cook the nougat; press.
Cure under weights 24 hours.
Cut into bars.

steps.do: Pour the honey into the medium heavy pan, clip on the thermometer and heat over medium, stirring often with a heatproof spatula, until it reaches 257°F (125°C) and the thick foam on the surface settles, about 10 minutes.
steps.look: Honey darkened slightly, the foam subsiding and the bubbles becoming slow and large.
steps.mistake: Cooking over high heat, which scorches the honey and makes the turrón bitter.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and keep stirring; if it smells burnt, start again with fresh honey.

steps.do: Whip the egg white with the salt in the smallest, deepest bowl your mixer takes for about 1 to 2 minutes, to soft peaks, timing it to be ready when the honey reaches 257°F (125°C).
steps.look: Soft, white, glossy peaks that fold over at the tip.
steps.mistake: Whipping too early, so the white sits and turns grainy and dry.
steps.fix: Re-whip it for a few seconds just before the syrup goes in.

steps.do: Boil the 1/3 cup (75 g) sugar and 2 tbsp (30 ml) water in the small pan over medium-high heat, without stirring, until the syrup reaches 300°F (150°C), the hard crack stage, about 6 minutes.
steps.look: A clear syrup with slow, thick bubbles, just beginning to turn straw at the edges.
steps.mistake: Stirring the syrup, which makes it crystallise into a cloudy mass.
steps.fix: Brush the inside of the pan with a wet pastry brush instead of stirring; if it crystallises, add water and start again.

steps.do: With the mixer running on medium-high, pour the sugar syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl into the egg white, then the hot honey, over about 1 minute. Whip for 1 minute more.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, sticky white mass that clings to the whisk.
steps.mistake: Pouring the syrup onto the whisk, which flings it onto the bowl as hard threads.
steps.fix: Pour down the side of the bowl; pick out any threads of sugar later.

steps.do: Set the bowl over the simmering bain-marie and stir with the sturdy spatula for 25 to 35 minutes, scraping the sides. Every 5 minutes from 20 minutes, drop 1/2 tsp (3 g) into cold water and test it.
steps.look: The mass slowly darkening to pale ivory gold, getting stiffer and pulling away from the bowl; the test piece snaps rather than bends.
steps.mistake: Stopping when it is still pliable in the water, so the turrón stays chewy rather than hard.
steps.fix: Keep stirring; it is ready only when the test piece cracks cleanly.

steps.do: Take the bowl off the heat and fold in the warm almonds and lemon zest quickly with the spatula, within 1 minute, before the nougat begins to stiffen.
steps.look: Almonds evenly coated in a thick, glossy nougat.
steps.mistake: Adding cold almonds, which chill the mass and make it seize into a lump.
steps.fix: Keep the almonds in a low oven until the moment you need them.

steps.do: Scrape the mixture into the wafer-lined frame, press it flat with an oiled spatula into the corners, cover with the second sheet of wafer, and press down hard with a board weighted with 2 lb (900 g) of tins.
steps.look: A level, compact slab about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick with no air gaps.
steps.mistake: Not pressing hard enough, so the turrón is full of holes and crumbles when cut.
steps.fix: Press while it is still warm; once cool it will not compact.

steps.do: Leave it under the weights at cool room temperature for 24 hours, then lift it out and cut into bars 1 inch (2.5 cm) wide with a heavy chef's knife, rocking the blade down firmly.
steps.look: A hard, glossy slab that snaps cleanly and shows the almonds in cross-section.
steps.mistake: Cutting before it has cured, so it is sticky and pulls.
steps.fix: Wait the full day; store the bars airtight in parchment.

science: Turrón's hardness depends on how much water is left in it. Honey is about 17 percent water, and cooking it to 257°F (125°C) concentrates its sugars. The sugar syrup at 300°F (150°C) is at the hard crack stage, with almost no water left. Whipped egg white traps air and gives a light structure; hot syrup cooks it. The long stir over a bain-marie slowly evaporates the remaining water without collapsing the foam. A test in cold water tells you when it is dry enough: if it bends, it is still wet; if it snaps, it is ready. Warm almonds keep the mass soft enough to fold.
plating: Cut into neat bars and serve on a plate with coffee, or wrap in parchment as a gift. Serve at the end of a meal with a glass of sweet wine.

pairing.drink: A Pedro Ximénez sherry or a Moscatel de Alicante: raisined sweetness matches honey and almond.
pairing.brennans: Barbadillo ‘Pale Cream’ Sherry NV: a gently sweet sherry from the Brennan's list that suits honey and almond.

variations: Use hazelnuts instead of almonds.
Add candied orange peel.
Make turrón de Jijona, a soft version ground into a paste.
safety: Sugar at 300°F (150°C) causes severe burns: pour carefully, wear long sleeves and keep children away.
Turrón is hard; warn guests to bite carefully.

title: Prinsesstårta
summary: Sweden's prinsesstårta: a light sponge layered with raspberry jam, vanilla custard and a tall dome of whipped cream, draped in a thin sheet of green marzipan and finished with a pink rose. It is in the course because it demands a smooth, tall dome of cream and a flawless marzipan drape with no cracks or folds.
equipment: 6 inch (15 cm) round cake tin, lined
Two sheets of parchment for rolling marzipan

ingredients.item: Vanilla pod, split (or 1 tsp (5 ml) extract)

mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C).
Make the custard first so it can chill.

timeline.do: Make the custard; chill.
Bake the sponge 25 minutes; cool.
Split, layer jam, custard and whipped cream; build the dome; chill 1 hour.
Roll and drape the marzipan; trim.
Add the rose; chill.
Slice.

steps.do: Make the custard: heat the milk with the vanilla until steaming. Whisk the yolks, sugar and cornflour; temper with the milk; return to the pan and cook, whisking, until it boils and thickens; hold 1 minute. Spread in a dish, cover the surface and chill.
steps.look: A thick, smooth custard flecked with vanilla.
steps.mistake: Lumps from not whisking constantly.
steps.fix: Sieve it.

steps.do: Whisk the eggs and sugar for 6 to 8 minutes until pale and thick enough to hold a ribbon for 3 seconds. Sift the flour, potato starch and baking powder over in three additions and fold gently.
steps.look: A light, airy batter with no streaks.
steps.mistake: Overmixing, which deflates the batter.
steps.fix: Fold with a large spatula.

steps.do: Bake the sponge in the lined tin at 350°F (180°C) for 25 minutes until golden and springy, then cool in the tin for 10 minutes and turn out onto a rack.
steps.look: A risen, golden sponge.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven early.
steps.fix: Wait 20 minutes.

steps.do: Split the sponge into three layers. Spread jam on the first layer, cover with the second, then beat the custard smooth and spread it on.
steps.look: Even layers of red jam and yellow custard.
steps.mistake: Too much custard, so the cake slides.
steps.fix: Use a thin layer.

steps.do: Whip the cream to firm peaks. Top with the third sponge layer, then pile the cream on and shape it into a tall, smooth dome with the palette knife. Chill 1 hour until firm.
steps.look: A tall, smooth dome of cream.
steps.mistake: A flat top with sharp edges, which splits the marzipan.
steps.fix: Build height in the centre and smooth the curve.

steps.do: Roll the marzipan between parchment sheets dusted with icing sugar into a circle about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick and 12 inches (30 cm) across.
steps.look: A thin, even circle of green marzipan.
steps.mistake: Rolling too thin, so it tears.
steps.fix: Keep it at 1/8 inch (3 mm).

steps.do: Peel off the top sheet, lift the marzipan on the bottom sheet and turn it over onto the dome, centring it so about 2 inches (5 cm) hangs down all round. Peel away the paper and smooth the marzipan downwards with your palms, easing out folds.
steps.look: A smooth drape with no air pockets or wrinkles.
steps.mistake: Pulling the marzipan down, so it tears at the top.
steps.fix: Lift and ease the folds, never pull.

steps.do: Trim the excess flush with the base using a sharp knife held straight down, about 1/4 inch (6 mm) from the board, and dust with icing sugar.
steps.look: A neat, smooth edge.
steps.mistake: Ragged trimming.
steps.fix: Use a sharp knife and cut straight down.

steps.do: Shape the pink marzipan into a rose and set it on top, with a few green leaves. Chill and slice with a hot knife.
steps.look: A pale green dome with a pink rose.
steps.mistake: Slicing with a cold knife.
steps.fix: Dip in hot water.

science: The sponge is light because air is whipped into eggs, and potato starch keeps the crumb tender and short, so it cuts cleanly. The custard is a starch-thickened cream that must boil so the cornflour gelatinises and the yolk enzymes are destroyed. Make small individual domes.

title: Doberge Cake
summary: New Orleans doberge cake: six thin layers of butter cake filled with chocolate custard, covered with buttercream and coated in a glossy poured chocolate glaze. It is in the course because it combines thin, even cake layers, a cooked custard filling and a poured glaze, and because it is the city's own adaptation of the Hungarian Dobos.
skills: a cooked chocolate or lemon custard filling
a poured fondant or ganache shell
equipment: Two 6 inch (15 cm) round cake tins, lined
Cake turntable and offset palette knife
Wire rack over a tray for glazing

ingredients.item: Golden syrup or light corn syrup

mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C).
Make the custard first so it chills.
Have the butter and eggs at room temperature.

timeline.do: Make the chocolate custard; chill 4 hours.
Bake the two cakes 25 to 30 minutes; cool.
Split each cake into three; layer with custard; chill 30 minutes.
Crumb coat with buttercream; chill 30 minutes.
Pour the glaze; chill 1 hour.
Slice the chilled cake into 4 portions with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between every cut.

steps.do: Make the chocolate custard: whisk the 1/3 cup (65 g) sugar, cornflour, cocoa and yolks with 1/4 cup (60 ml) of the milk in a bowl until smooth. Heat the remaining milk until steaming, whisk a ladle into the yolks, then pour everything back and cook over medium heat, whisking constantly, until it boils and thickens; keep it bubbling for 1 full minute. Off the heat, whisk in the 2 oz (55 g) chopped chocolate.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, dark custard that holds the marks of the whisk and tastes of chocolate, not raw starch.
steps.mistake: Taking it off at the first thickening, so the starch is not cooked and the filling turns runny in the fridge.
steps.fix: Return it to the heat and boil for a full minute, whisking hard.

steps.do: Press cling film onto the surface of the custard and chill for at least 4 hours until cold and firm.
steps.look: A firm, set custard with no skin.
steps.mistake: Leaving it uncovered, so a rubbery skin forms and leaves lumps when spread.
steps.fix: Strain lumpy custard through a sieve or whisk it smooth before use.

steps.do: Cream the soft butter and 3/4 cup (150 g) sugar in the mixer on medium-high for 4 to 5 minutes, scraping the bowl twice, until pale and fluffy. Beat in the eggs one at a time, 30 seconds each, then the vanilla.
steps.look: A light, almost white mixture that has noticeably grown in volume.
steps.mistake: Using cold butter, so the mixture never fluffs and the cake is heavy.
steps.fix: Leave the butter out longer, or warm the bowl briefly with a hot towel and keep beating.

steps.do: Whisk the flour, baking powder and salt together. Add to the butter mixture in three parts, alternating with the buttermilk in two parts, mixing on low only until each addition disappears.
steps.look: A smooth, thick, creamy batter with no streaks of flour.
steps.mistake: Beating on high after the flour goes in, which develops gluten and gives a tough, tunnelled crumb.
steps.fix: Mix on low and finish by hand with a spatula.

steps.do: Divide the batter equally between the two lined 6 inch (15 cm) tins, about 11 1/2 oz (325 g) each, level the tops and bake at 350°F (180°C) for 25 to 30 minutes until a skewer comes out clean and the tops spring back.
steps.look: Golden cakes that have just started to pull away from the sides of the tins.
steps.mistake: Overfilling one tin, so the layers end up different heights.
steps.fix: Weigh the batter into the tins.

steps.do: Cool the cakes in their tins for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a rack and cool completely, at least 1 hour. Level any domed tops with the serrated knife.
steps.look: Two flat, cold cakes.
steps.mistake: Splitting warm cakes, which tear and crumble.
steps.fix: Chill the cakes for 30 minutes to firm them before splitting.

steps.do: Mark each cake into three equal heights with cocktail sticks pushed in round the side, then split it with the serrated knife into three layers about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick, turning the cake on the turntable as you cut.
steps.look: Six thin, even layers.
steps.mistake: Cutting freehand, so some layers are thick and some break.
steps.fix: Use the sticks as a guide and keep the knife level; a broken layer goes in the middle.

steps.do: Beat the chilled custard smooth. Set the first layer on the cake board and spread about 1/4 cup (60 g) custard to within 1/4 inch (6 mm) of the edge. Repeat with all six layers, pressing each gently, and finish with a cake layer. Chill 30 minutes.
steps.look: A straight, level stack with thin dark lines of custard.
steps.mistake: Spreading custard to the very edge, so it squeezes out under the weight of the layers.
steps.fix: Leave the border; scrape off any custard that oozes before crumb coating.

steps.do: Make the buttercream: beat the soft butter, icing sugar and cocoa on medium for 3 minutes until smooth and fluffy. Spread a thin crumb coat over the top and sides of the cake, scraping it smooth with the bench scraper. Chill 30 minutes.
steps.look: A thin, even chocolate coat that seals in every crumb.
steps.mistake: A thick coat that leaves a lumpy surface under the glaze.
steps.fix: Scrape it thinner; the glaze needs a smooth, cold, firm base.

steps.do: Make the glaze: heat the 1/2 cup (120 ml) cream and the syrup until steaming, pour over the 4 oz (115 g) chopped chocolate, stand 2 minutes and stir until smooth. Cool, stirring now and then, to 90°F (32°C).
steps.look: A smooth, glossy glaze that runs off a spoon in a thick stream.
steps.mistake: Pouring it hot, so it melts the buttercream and runs thin.
steps.fix: Wait for 90°F (32°C); if it gets too thick, warm it over water for 5 seconds.

steps.do: Set the cold cake on the rack over a tray. Pour the glaze onto the centre and let it run over the edge, helping it with one pass of the palette knife across the top. Chill 1 hour, then slice into 4 portions with a knife dipped in hot water and wiped between cuts.
steps.look: A glossy, even coat and slices showing six thin layers striped with dark custard.
steps.mistake: Smoothing again and again, which leaves knife marks in the setting glaze.
steps.fix: Pour generously and make one pass only; scrape up the drips for another use.

science: The cake is a creamed butter cake: beating butter and sugar traps air, and baking powder produces gas that expands those bubbles in the oven. Buttermilk's acid reacts with the baking powder and tenderises the crumb. The custard is thickened by cornflour and egg, and must boil so the starch gelatinises and the yolk enzymes are destroyed. The glaze is a ganache: chocolate melted into hot cream forms an emulsion, and a little syrup adds gloss and keeps it supple. Pouring at 90°F (32°C) gives a glaze fluid enough to flow but cool enough not to melt the buttercream.
plating: Set a tall slice on its side on a plate to show the six layers. Serve with a cup of coffee and a small spoon of whipped cream.

pairing.drink: A New Orleans coffee with chicory, or a tawny port: bitterness or nutty sweetness balances the chocolate.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory: Brennan's own chicory coffee, the city's classic partner for a slice of doberge.

variations: Lemon doberge: lemon custard and a lemon fondant glaze.
Half and half: one half chocolate and one half lemon, as often sold in New Orleans.
Caramel doberge with a caramel custard.
safety: The custard boils, which makes the yolks safe.
Keep the cake refrigerated and eat within 3 days.

title: Baked Alaska
summary: Baked Alaska: a dome of homemade vanilla ice cream frozen rock hard on a disc of sponge, armoured in thick Italian meringue and browned in a blazing oven or with a torch, so it arrives hot outside and frozen within. It is in the course because it draws together churning, a cooked meringue and split-second timing, and because it is a piece of dining room theatre worth understanding.
skills: homemade ice cream frozen hard in a dome
an Italian meringue piped and torched
equipment: Ice cream maker with its bowl frozen for 24 hours
Heavy saucepan, whisk and an instant-read thermometer
Bowl 5 inches (13 cm) across, about 2 1/2 cups (600 ml), lined with cling film
Small heavy saucepan and a sugar thermometer
Piping bag with a large star or plain tip, or a palette knife
Ovenproof serving plate or a baking tray lined with parchment
Long knife and a jug of hot water

ingredients.item: Vanilla pod, split (or 2 tsp (10 ml) extract)

mise: Freeze the ice cream maker bowl for 24 hours.
Clear space in the freezer for the bowl and then the finished dessert on a flat tray.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C) for the sponge.

timeline.do: Make and churn the ice cream; pack into the lined bowl and freeze overnight.
Bake the sponge; cool and wrap.
Unmould the ice cream onto the sponge; freeze 1 hour.
Make the Italian meringue; cover completely; freeze at least 1 hour.
Heat the oven to 475°F (250°C).
Bake 3 to 4 minutes or torch.
Serve at once, cutting with a hot knife.

steps.do: Make the ice cream base: heat the milk, cream, salt and vanilla pod and seeds until steaming, about 180°F (82°C). Whisk the yolks and sugar until pale, temper with a ladle of the hot milk, return to the pan and cook over low heat, stirring, until it coats a spoon at 175 to 180°F (79 to 82°C).
steps.look: A smooth custard that coats the spatula and holds a clean line drawn through it with a finger.
steps.mistake: Overheating past 185°F (85°C), which scrambles the yolks into flecks.
steps.fix: Pour at once into a cold bowl and blend with a stick blender, then strain.

steps.do: Strain the custard into a bowl set in iced water, stir until cool, then cover and chill for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. Churn in the ice cream maker for 20 to 25 minutes until thick, like soft-serve.
steps.look: Thick, creamy ice cream that holds a ribbon.
steps.mistake: Churning a warm base, which never thickens.
steps.fix: Chill longer; the base should be below 40°F (4°C).

steps.do: Pack the ice cream into the film-lined bowl, pressing out air pockets with the back of a spoon, level the top, cover and freeze overnight until rock hard.
steps.look: A solid, smooth dome of ice cream.
steps.mistake: Leaving air pockets, which make the dome collapse when cut.
steps.fix: Press firmly in layers as you fill.

steps.do: Make the sponge: whisk the eggs and sugar on high speed for 6 to 8 minutes until pale and thick. Fold in the flour in three additions, then the melted butter, and bake in the lined 6 inch (15 cm) tin at 350°F (180°C) for 18 to 20 minutes until springy. Cool.
steps.look: A light, golden sponge about 1 inch (2.5 cm) tall.
steps.mistake: Deflating the batter by stirring instead of folding.
steps.fix: Fold gently with a large spatula; the next one will rise better.

steps.do: Set the sponge on the ovenproof plate and brush it with the liqueur, if using. Dip the ice cream bowl in warm water for 5 seconds, turn the dome out onto the sponge, peel off the film, and trim the sponge to leave a 1/2 inch (1 cm) border. Freeze 1 hour.
steps.look: A frozen dome sitting neatly on its sponge base.
steps.mistake: Letting the ice cream soften, so it slumps.
steps.fix: Work fast and return it to the freezer at once.

steps.do: Make the Italian meringue: boil the sugar and water without stirring to 244°F (118°C). When the syrup reaches 230°F (110°C), start whipping the whites with the cream of tartar to soft peaks. Pour the hot syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl into the whites with the mixer running, then whip on high for 8 to 10 minutes until glossy, stiff and cool.
steps.look: A thick, glossy meringue that stands in stiff peaks and feels barely warm.
steps.mistake: Pouring syrup onto the whisk, which spins it into sugar threads.
steps.fix: Pour down the side; if threads form, pick them out.

steps.do: Working quickly, pipe or spread the meringue over the frozen dome in a layer at least 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick, sealing it right down to the plate so no sponge or ice cream shows. Pull the surface into peaks or pipe rosettes.
steps.look: A complete, thick shell of meringue with no gaps, swirled into peaks.
steps.mistake: Leaving a gap at the base, where the heat gets in and melts the ice cream.
steps.fix: Run the palette knife round the base to seal it to the plate.

steps.do: Freeze the finished dessert, uncovered, for at least 1 hour, or up to 2 days.
steps.look: A firm, frozen meringue shell.
steps.mistake: Covering it with film, which sticks to the meringue.
steps.fix: Freeze uncovered; once frozen, cover loosely with a tall box.

steps.do: To serve, bake in the 475°F (250°C) oven on the top shelf for 3 to 4 minutes until the peaks are golden brown, or torch the surface evenly, holding the flame 3 inches (8 cm) away.
steps.look: Golden tips and pale valleys, a smell of toasted marshmallow.
steps.mistake: Baking too long, so the ice cream melts inside.
steps.fix: Watch it every 30 seconds; take it out as soon as the tips colour.

steps.do: Cut at once into 4 wedges with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped between each cut, and serve.
steps.look: A hot, toasted meringue shell, cold ice cream and soft sponge in every slice.
steps.mistake: Waiting at the table, so the ice cream softens.
steps.fix: Have plates and the hot knife ready before it comes out of the oven.

science: The trick is insulation. Meringue is mostly air trapped in a network of egg protein and sugar, and air conducts heat very poorly, so a thick, sealed meringue shell protects the frozen ice cream for the few minutes the oven browns the surface. Italian meringue is made with syrup at 244°F (118°C), which partly cooks the whites and dissolves the sugar, giving a dense, stable foam that does not weep. The sponge at the base insulates the ice cream from the plate. Ice cream stays smooth because churning freezes it quickly while beating in air, keeping ice crystals small, and the sugar and fat lower its freezing point.
plating: Bring the whole Alaska to the table on its plate, golden and smoking slightly, and cut it there. Lay each wedge on its side on a cold plate so the browned shell, white meringue, vanilla ice cream and sponge show, and add a spoon of fruit sauce or a few berries.

pairing.drink: A demi-sec Champagne or a sweet sparkling Moscato: gentle sweetness and bubbles refresh after rich meringue and ice cream.
pairing.brennans: Cherries Jubilee: another Brennan's dessert built on table-side theatre, flamed in the dining room just as a Baked Alaska can be.

variations: Flambé it at the table with warmed rum poured over and lit.
Use two layers of ice cream, such as raspberry sorbet and vanilla.
Make individual Alaskas on rounds of sponge.
safety: Syrup at 244°F (118°C) does not fully pasteurise the whites, so use pasteurised egg whites; the ice cream custard is cooked to a safe 160°F (71°C) or above.
Hot sugar syrup causes serious burns: pour carefully and keep children away.
A 475°F (250°C) oven and a blowtorch are both fierce: use oven gloves and keep the torch flame away from your hand and anything flammable.

title: Sachertorte
summary: Vienna's Sachertorte: a dense, fine-crumbed chocolate sponge split and filled with apricot jam, painted with more jam and enrobed in a glossy chocolate glaze cooked with sugar syrup, served with unsweetened whipped cream. It is in the course because it requires folding a whisked batter into melted chocolate without losing air, a glaze cooked to the right point, and the precision of tempering chocolate for its decoration.
skills: a chocolate sponge raised with meringue
a cooked chocolate glaze poured in one motion
equipment: 6 inch (15 cm) springform tin, lined and buttered
Heatproof bowls and a pan for melting chocolate
Small saucepan and a sugar thermometer
Small piping cone or a zip bag

ingredients.item: Dark chocolate, 60 to 70 percent, for cake

mise: Heat the oven to 340°F (170°C).
Melt the cake chocolate over barely simmering water and cool to about 95°F (35°C).
Have the butter and eggs at room temperature.

timeline.do: Bake the cake 40 to 45 minutes; cool upside down overnight.
Split, fill and coat with warm jam; let it set 1 hour.
Cook and pour the glaze; set 2 hours.
Temper chocolate and pipe the decoration.
Slice with a hot knife; serve with whipped cream.

steps.do: Beat the butter and icing sugar for 3 minutes until pale and creamy. Beat in the yolks one at a time, then the cooled melted chocolate, vanilla and salt.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, chocolate-brown mixture.
steps.mistake: Adding hot chocolate, which melts the butter and makes the batter greasy.
steps.fix: Cool the chocolate to about 95°F (35°C) first.

steps.do: In a clean bowl, whip the egg whites to soft peaks, then add the caster sugar gradually and whip to firm, glossy peaks that bend slightly at the tip, about 4 minutes.
steps.look: Glossy peaks that hold but curl over at the tip.
steps.mistake: Overwhipping to dry, grainy peaks that will not fold in.
steps.fix: Fold in a spoonful of liquid white and whisk briefly to loosen.

steps.do: Fold a third of the whites into the chocolate mixture to loosen it, then fold in the rest in two additions alternately with the flour, cutting down through the centre and turning the bowl.
steps.look: A smooth, airy batter with no streaks of white.
steps.mistake: Stirring, which knocks out the air and makes a heavy cake.
steps.fix: Fold gently with a large spatula, about 30 strokes in all.

steps.do: Pour into the tin, level the top and bake for 40 to 45 minutes until a skewer comes out with a few moist crumbs. Turn out upside down on the rack and cool overnight for a flat top.
steps.look: A risen cake with a slightly cracked top that settles as it cools.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven in the first 25 minutes, so the cake sinks.
steps.fix: Keep the door closed until a skewer test at 35 minutes.

steps.do: Trim the top flat if needed and split the cake into two layers with the serrated knife. Spread half the warm jam on the bottom layer and set the top on it.
steps.look: Two even layers with a thin line of jam.
steps.mistake: Splitting a warm cake, which crumbles.
steps.fix: Cool it completely, overnight is best.

steps.do: Brush the warm jam over the top and sides in a thin, even layer, and leave to set for 1 hour.
steps.look: A shiny, tacky coat of apricot over the whole cake.
steps.mistake: Using cold jam, which tears the crumb.
steps.fix: Warm it until runny and sieve it.

steps.do: Make the glaze: boil the sugar and water to 225°F (107°C). Take it off the heat, add the chopped chocolate and stir until smooth. Keep stirring as it cools to about 100°F (38°C), when it thickens and coats a spoon in an even, opaque layer.
steps.look: A glossy, thick glaze that coats a spoon like pouring cream.
steps.mistake: Pouring it too hot, so it runs off thin and dull; or too cool, so it sets in ridges.
steps.fix: Reheat gently or cool longer, testing on a spoon.

steps.do: Set the cake on the rack over a tray. Pour all the glaze over the centre in one motion and spread it once over the top with the palette knife so it flows down the sides. Do not touch it again. Leave to set for 2 hours.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy coat with no bare spots.
steps.mistake: Going back to smooth it, which leaves marks.
steps.fix: Scrape the excess from the tray and keep it for decoration.

steps.do: Temper the decoration chocolate: melt two-thirds of it to 115 to 120°F (46 to 49°C), stir in the remaining chopped chocolate until it cools to 81 to 82°F (27 to 28°C), then warm it gently to 88 to 90°F (31 to 32°C).
steps.look: Glossy chocolate that sets crisp with a snap on the tip of a knife in 3 minutes.
steps.mistake: Letting it go above 90°F (32°C), which loses the temper and leaves it dull and streaky.
steps.fix: Cool it again with more chopped chocolate and rewarm.

steps.do: Put the tempered chocolate into the piping cone and pipe the word Sacher or a simple design on the cake.
steps.look: Glossy, crisp lettering.
steps.mistake: Piping with untempered chocolate, which smears.
steps.fix: Practise first on parchment.

steps.do: Whip the cream to soft peaks without sugar. Slice the cake with a hot knife and serve each slice with a spoon of cream.
steps.look: Clean slices showing the jam line, with soft cream alongside.
steps.mistake: Sweetening the cream, which makes the plate too sweet.
steps.fix: Keep the cream plain; it balances the cake.

science: Sachertorte is a whisked chocolate sponge: the air in the whipped whites lifts it, and folding preserves the bubbles while the melted chocolate and butter make the crumb dense and fine. The jam acts as a moisture barrier and glue, keeping the cake moist under the glaze. The glaze is a sugar syrup cooked to 225°F (107°C) and blended with chocolate; stirring as it cools encourages fine sugar crystals and gives the glaze its glossy, slightly firm finish. Tempering aligns the cocoa butter into its stable crystal form (form V), which sets with a snap and a shine; untempered chocolate sets soft and streaky.
plating: Set a slice on a plate, glossy top and cut face showing the thin line of apricot, with a generous spoon of unsweetened whipped cream beside it. Serve with a cup of coffee, the Viennese way.

pairing.drink: A Viennese melange coffee, or a Banyuls: the coffee cuts the richness, and the sweet red wine matches chocolate and apricot.
pairing.brennans: Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva NV: a sweet red wine from the Brennan's list, the classic partner for dark chocolate.

variations: Use raspberry jam instead of apricot.
Make individual Sacher cubes for a buffet.
Use a simple ganache glaze if a cooked glaze seems daunting.
safety: Sugar syrup at 225°F (107°C) burns: stir with a long spoon and keep children away.
Keep the cake at cool room temperature and eat within 4 days.

title: Macarons
summary: French macarons: smooth, domed almond meringue shells with ruffled feet, made by the Italian meringue method, folded to the exact consistency, piped, rested, baked and filled with dark chocolate ganache. It is in the course because few things in pastry are as unforgiving: a few strokes too many or too few in the folding and the shells crack, spread or stay hollow.
equipment: Small heavy saucepan and a sugar thermometer
Piping bag with a 1/2 inch (1 cm) plain tip
Two heavy baking trays lined with parchment or silicone mats

ingredients.item: Egg whites, aged 24 to 48 hours in the fridge, divided
ingredients.metric: about 75 g, as two 37 g portions

ingredients.item: Dark chocolate, 60 to 70 percent, chopped, for ganache

mise: Separate the egg whites a day ahead, cover and keep them in the fridge, then bring them to room temperature for 1 hour before using; weigh them into two equal portions.
Pulse the ground almonds and icing sugar in the food processor for 15 seconds, then sift; discard any coarse bits left in the sieve.
Place the template under the parchment.

timeline.do: Separate and age the whites.
Make the shells; rest 30 to 60 minutes; bake; cool.
Make the ganache; fill the shells.
Mature the filled macarons in the fridge for 24 hours.
Bring to room temperature.
Serve.

steps.do: Mix the sifted almond and icing sugar with the first portion of egg white to a thick paste.
steps.look: A thick, stiff almond paste.
steps.mistake: Lumps of almond.
steps.fix: Press them out with the spatula.

steps.do: Boil the caster sugar and water to 244°F (118°C). When it reaches 230°F (110°C), start whipping the second portion of white to soft peaks.
steps.look: A clear syrup reaching temperature as the whites hold soft peaks.
steps.mistake: Starting the whites too late or too early.
steps.fix: Lower the heat under the syrup if the whites are behind.

steps.do: Pour the hot syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl into the whipping whites. Whip on high for 5 minutes until glossy and stiff, and cooled to about 120°F (49°C).
steps.look: A thick, glossy meringue holding stiff peaks.
steps.mistake: Pouring onto the whisk.
steps.fix: Pour down the side.

steps.do: Fold a third of the meringue into the almond paste to loosen it, then fold in the rest. Continue folding (macaronage), pressing the batter against the side of the bowl, until it flows off the spatula in a thick, unbroken ribbon and a figure of eight drawn with it sinks back in about 10 seconds.
steps.look: A glossy batter like slow-flowing lava, holding a ribbon.
steps.mistake: Overmixing, so it runs thin and the shells spread; or undermixing, so they crack and have peaks.
steps.fix: Test often; stop as soon as it ribbons.

steps.do: Pipe 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) rounds onto the template, holding the bag straight up 1/2 inch (1 cm) above the tray and stopping pressure before lifting.
steps.look: Smooth, round discs with small peaks that settle within 30 seconds.
steps.mistake: Piping at an angle, which makes oval shells.
steps.fix: Hold the bag vertically.

steps.do: Tap the trays firmly on the counter 3 or 4 times to release bubbles, and pop any remaining with a toothpick.
steps.look: Smooth, flat discs with no bubbles.
steps.mistake: Skipping this, so the shells crack.
steps.fix: Tap firmly.

steps.do: Rest the piped shells at room temperature for 30 to 60 minutes until a skin forms and they are no longer sticky to a light touch.
steps.look: A matte, dry skin.
steps.mistake: Baking before a skin forms, which makes them crack.
steps.fix: Wait longer in a humid kitchen.

steps.do: Bake one tray at a time at 300°F (150°C) for 13 to 15 minutes until the feet are risen and the tops do not move when gently pushed.
steps.look: Smooth, domed shells with ruffled feet.
steps.mistake: Oven too hot, so they brown or crack.
steps.fix: Use an oven thermometer and adjust.

steps.do: Cool the shells completely on the tray, about 20 minutes, then peel the parchment away from the shells rather than lifting the shells off the paper.
steps.look: Shells that release cleanly.
steps.mistake: Peeling warm shells, which stick.
steps.fix: Cool fully.

steps.do: Make the ganache: heat the cream until steaming, pour over the chocolate, stand 2 minutes, stir until smooth, add the butter. Cool until thick enough to pipe, about 30 minutes.
steps.look: A glossy, thick ganache.
steps.mistake: Using it while runny.
steps.fix: Cool longer, or chill 10 minutes.

steps.do: Pair shells by size. Pipe a ganache mound on one shell of each pair and sandwich with the other, pressing gently. Chill for 24 hours before serving.
steps.look: Even sandwiches with the filling just visible.
steps.mistake: Serving the same day, when the shells are crisp and dry.
steps.fix: Mature them for 24 hours.

science: A macaron shell is a meringue stabilised with ground almonds and sugar. The Italian method cooks the whites with hot syrup, making a stable, glossy meringue. Macaronage deflates the meringue just enough that the batter flows and levels itself, but still holds enough air to rise. Resting forms a dry skin on top, so that in the oven the steam escapes from the base, lifting the shell and forming the ruffled feet. Aged egg whites have lost some water, making a stronger foam. Maturing the filled macarons lets moisture from the ganache soften the shells into a chewy centre.
plating: Arrange the macarons on a white plate in a neat row or a small pyramid, the feet facing outward. Serve with coffee or a glass of Champagne.

pairing.drink: A Champagne, or a strong espresso: the bubbles cleanse the palate, and the coffee balances the sweet shells.
pairing.brennans: Krug ‘Grand Cuvée’ Brut NV (375 ml): a rich Champagne from the Brennan's list with toasty depth for chocolate macarons.

variations: Raspberry macarons with raspberry jam and white chocolate ganache.
Pistachio macarons with pistachio buttercream.
Salted caramel macarons.
safety: Age the egg whites covered in the fridge, never at room temperature, and bring them up to temperature only for the hour before use.
The shells contain raw egg white that is cooked by the syrup and the oven.
Hot sugar syrup causes serious burns: pour carefully.
